nodes.name: Connect to FalkorDB
nodes.content:
FalkorDB

Ultra-fast, Multi-tenant Graph Database

Powering Generative AI, Agent Memory, Cloud Security, and Fraud Detection


![FalkorDB GitHub Repo - Video - 640x365](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/131867d4-fa2b-41f8-ac72-5c5f6eaf4e12)
## UNIQUE FEATURES Our goal is to build a high-performance Knowledge Graph tailored for Large Language Models (LLMs), prioritizing exceptionally low latency to ensure fast and efficient information delivery through our Graph Database. 🆕 [FalkorDB](https://www.falkordb.com/) is the first **queryable [Property Graph](https://github.com/opencypher/openCypher/blob/master/docs/property-graph-model.adoc) database to leverage sparse matrices** for representing the [adjacency matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjacency_matrix) in graphs and [linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjacency_matrix) for querying. ### Key Features * **Sparse Matrix Representation**: Utilizes sparse matrices to represent adjacency matrices, optimizing storage and performance. * **Linear Algebra Querying**: Employs linear algebra for query execution, enhancing computational efficiency. * **Property Graph Model Compliance**: Supports nodes and relationships with attributes, adhering to the Property Graph Model. * **OpenCypher Support:** Compatible with [OpenCypher](https://github.com/opencypher/openCypher/blob/master/docs/property-graph-model.adoc) query language, including proprietary extensions for advanced querying capabilities. >Explore FalkorDB in action by visiting the [Demos](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/tree/master/demo). ## GET STARTED ### Step 1 To quickly try out FalkorDB, launch an instance using docker: ``` docker run -p 6379:6379 -p 3000:3000 -it --rm -v ./data:/var/lib/falkordb/data falkordb/falkordb ``` ### Step 2 Then, open your browser and navigate to `http://localhost:3000`. You can also interact with FalkorDB using any of the supported [Client Libraries](https://docs.falkordb.com/clients.html) ### MotoGP League Example In this example, we'll use the [FalkorDB Python client](https://pypi.org/project/FalkorDB/) to create a small graph representing a subset of motorcycle riders and teams participating in the MotoGP league. After creating the graph, we'll query the data to explore its structure and relationships. ```python from falkordb import FalkorDB # Connect to FalkorDB db = FalkorDB(host='localhost', port=6379) # Create the 'MotoGP' graph g = db.select_graph('MotoGP') g.query("""CREATE (:Rider {name:'Valentino Rossi'})-[:rides]->(:Team {name:'Yamaha'}), (:Rider {name:'Dani Pedrosa'})-[:rides]->(:Team {name:'Honda'}), (:Rider {name:'Andrea Dovizioso'})-[:rides]->(:Team {name:'Ducati'})""") # Query which riders represents Yamaha? res = g.query("""MATCH (r:Rider)-[:rides]->(t:Team) WHERE t.name = 'Yamaha' RETURN r.name""") for row in res.result_set: print(row[0]) # Prints: "Valentino Rossi" # Query how many riders represent team Ducati ? res = g.query("""MATCH (r:Rider)-[:rides]->(t:Team {name:'Ducati'}) RETURN count(r)""") print(res.result_set[0][0]) # Prints: 1 ``` ## USING FALKORDB You can call FalkorDB's commands from any Redis client. Here are several methods: ### With `redis-cli` ```sh $ redis-cli 127.0.0.1:6379> GRAPH.QUERY social "CREATE (:person {name: 'roi', age: 33, gender: 'male', status: 'married'})" ``` ### With any other client You can interact with FalkorDB using your client's ability to send raw Redis commands. >Note: Depending on your client of choice, the exact method for doing that may vary. #### Example: Using FalkorDB with a Python client This code snippet shows how to use FalkorDB with from Python using [falkordb-py](https://github.com/FalkorDB/falkordb-py): ```Python from falkordb import FalkorDB # Connect to FalkorDB db = FalkorDB(host='localhost', port=6379) # Select the social graph g = db.select_graph('social') reply = g.query("CREATE (:person {name:'roi', age:33, gender:'male', status:'married'})") ``` ## CLIENT LIBRARIES >Note: Some languages have client libraries that provide support for FalkorDB's commands: ### Official Clients | Project | Language | License | Author | nodes.name: 6.0.0: server panics (`src/reply.rs:655:58`, `Option::unwrap()` on `None`) when a null precedes an aggregate in RETURN
nodes.content:
## Summary

On `falkordb/falkordb:6.0.0`, a query whose `RETURN` has a null value in a column before an aggregate (`count`, `collect`) panics the module and brings down the whole server. The null can be a literal or a missing property. The smallest reproduction needs no data:

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN null AS x, count(1) AS n"
```

The same queries return the expected rows on `v4.20.4`.

## Environment

- Image: `falkordb/falkordb:6.0.0` (`sha256:92fbda814970a648b1fd80835bff221766bccd0f0ce958bc58a62976fea06620`, also `latest` as of 2026-09-29)
- Redis 8.10.2 (as reported by the image)
- Docker Desktop on macOS, Apple Silicon (linux/arm64). Seen on two machines.
- Default configuration (`docker run -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb:6.0.0`)

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
docker run -d --name f6 -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb:6.0.0
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN null AS x, count(1) AS n"
# Error: Server closed the connection
docker logs f6 | grep -A3 panic
```

With data, a missing property as the null:

```bash
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:B {id:'b'})"
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (b:B) RETURN b.id AS k, b.missing AS x, count(b) AS n"
# Error: Server closed the connection
```

## Expected

One row each, as on `v4.20.4`:

| query | v4.20.4 result |
|---|---|
| `RETURN null AS x, count(1) AS n` | `x = null, n = 1` |
| `MATCH (b:B) RETURN b.id AS k, b.missing AS x, count(b) AS n` | `k = 'b', x = null, n = 1` |

## Actual

The server process exits:

```
# <module> FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/reply.rs:655:58:
called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value
Backtrace:
   0: <std::backtrace::Backtrace>::create
   1: falkordb::module_init::graph_init::{closure#0}
   2: std::panicking::panic_with_hook
   3: std::panicking::panic_handler::{closure#0}
   4: std::sys::backtrace::__rust_end_short_backtrace::<std::panicking::panic_handler::{closure#0}, !>
   5: __rustc::rust_begin_unwind
   6: core::panicking::panic_fmt
   7: core::panicking::panic
   8: core::option::unwrap_failed
   9: falkordb::reply::reply_compact
  10: falkordb::graph_core::execute_query
  11: <falkordb::graph_core::query_mut::{closure#0} as core::ops::function::FnOnce<()>>::call_once::{shim:vtable#0}
  12: <graph::threadpool::ThreadPool>::new::{closure#0}
  ...
```

With `restart: unless-stopped` the container comes back, and the next identical query crashes it again. One of our machines logged dozens of restarts in two hours.

## What triggers it

Each case was run three times on a fresh server, with the same result every time:

| query (on `CREATE (:A {id:'a'})-[:R]->(:B {id:'b'})`) | 6.0.0 |
|---|---|
| `RETURN null AS x, count(1) AS n` | **crash** |
| `RETURN null AS x, collect(1) AS n` | **crash** |
| `MATCH (b:B) RETURN b.id AS k, b.missing AS x, count(b) AS n` | **crash** |
| `RETURN count(1) AS n, null AS x` (null after the aggregate) | ok |
| `WITH null AS x RETURN x, count(1) AS n` (null projected first) | ok |
| `RETURN 1 AS x, count(1) AS n` (not null) | ok |
| `RETURN null AS x` (no aggregate) | ok |
| `MATCH (b:B) RETURN b.missing AS x, count(b) AS n` | ok |
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(b:B) RETURN b.id AS k, b.missing AS x, collect(a.id) AS n` | ok |

- The crash also happens with `GRAPH.RO_QUERY`, and without `--compact` (the verbose reply).
- It's not every null grouping key: the last two rows survive. So we can't say exactly which condition matters. What all the crashing cases share is a null grouping key before an aggregate.

## Where we hit it

A read query in our application, against a graph where the frame had no `maxDurationMin` property:

```cypher
MATCH (f)-[t:TRIGGERS_FRAME]->(fr:Frame) WHERE f.id IN $factors AND t.status = 'active'
OPTIONAL MATCH (fr)-[:ALLOWS_POSITION]->(p:Category)
RETURN fr.id AS frame, fr.name AS name, collect(DISTINCT f.id) AS triggeredBy, collect(DISTINCT t.strength) AS strengths,
       collect(DISTINCT p.id) AS positions, fr.maxDurationMin AS maxDurationMin, t.sourceIds AS sourceIds
```

It's sent from falkordb-py (`graph.query`, `--compact`), and it works on 4.x. As a workaround we have pinned `falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.4`.

## Related: 4.x can't start on data written by 6.0.0

After running 6.0.0, going back to `v4.20.4` on the same data volume fails at startup:

```
# Can't handle RDB format version 15
# Error reading the RDB base file appendonly.aof.1.base.rdb, AOF loading aborted
```

That may be expected for a major version, but it means users who got 6.0.0 through `latest` can't simply pin back without discarding their data. A note in the 6.0.0 release notes would help.

nodes.name: docs: correct tensor compound key encoding overview
nodes.content: The module-level Compound Key Encoding section still describes `(src << 32) | dst`, while `compound_key` now splits each endpoint into high bits that select an `me` block and low 30 bits that form a 60-bit row key. Update the overview to match the implementation, correct the node 3 → 7 hexadecimal example, and clarify that edge IDs occupy columns within the selected block. Validation: `git diff --check` passes; verified the hexadecimal example and confirmed executable code is unchanged. No runtime tests run (documentation-only change). --- ## Summary by cubic Corrects the compound key encoding overview in the `tensor.rs` module docs to match the actual implementation. The docs now explain how endpoint IDs split into high bits for block selection and low 30 bits for a 60-bit row key, fixes the hexadecimal example, and notes that edge IDs are stored as columns within the selected block. Written for commit ca9fb89609dd87bfc8934b135095f2a913bb4f9d. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Documentation** * Clarified how multi-edge row keys are organized into blocks and how larger endpoint IDs select different blocks.

nodes.name: fix(runtime): re-bind grouping keys after accumulator unbind (#3150)
nodes.content: In AggregateOp::next, internal aggregate accumulator variables are unbound so they do not leak to downstream operators. However, accumulator slot IDs can coincide with grouping keys (or pre-projection key variables) due to slot ID reuse. When an accumulator slot ID coincided with a grouping key that evaluated to NULL, the key column was left unbound and dropped during columnar finish as Column::Unbound. This caused a server panic in src/reply.rs when unwrapping the return column value. - Re-bind grouping keys (self.keys) after unbinding accumulators in AggregateOp::next. - Guard batch.value_at() in reply_result with .unwrap_or(Value::Null) to prevent process panics on unbound columns in query results. - Add regression test test10_null_preceding_aggregate in tests/flow/test_null_handling.py. Fixes #3150 --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes a server panic when a query returns a NULL column before an aggregate (e.g. `RETURN null AS x, count(1)`). Accumulator slot IDs could be reused for grouping keys, so unbinding accumulators in `AggregateOp::next` also unbound NULL grouping keys, leaving the column `Unbound` and crashing `reply_result` when unwrapping the value. - Re-binds grouping keys after unbinding accumulators so NULL keys survive columnar finish. - Replaces the `unwrap()` on `batch.value_at()` in `src/reply.rs` with `unwrap_or(Value::Null)` to prevent panics on unbound columns. - Adds regression test `test10_null_preceding_aggregate` covering `RETURN` projections and `MATCH` with missing properties, using a dedicated graph for idempotency. Written for commit ac250a9386804c9846bb2d0cff90211b48c31ff2. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Fixed aggregate query results so grouping values are preserved when groups are returned alongside aggregate values. * Queries that produce a missing value now return it as `null` instead of failing. This also fixes results for projections with a missing property before an aggregate, including `count` and `collect` queries. * These fixes help ensure query results remain available when grouping keys, null projections, or missing properties occur alongside aggregation.

nodes.name: fix(restore): return an error for malformed GRAPH.RESTORE payloads
nodes.content: Closes #3168 ## What `GRAPH.RESTORE` crashes the server when the payload is empty or cut short. This PR makes it return an error instead. ## Why it happens `GRAPH.RESTORE` decodes with `BufferedReader::from_slice`, which sets `rdb` to null. When the reader runs out of bytes, `ensure_available` calls `load_chunk`, and that calls `raw::load_string_buffer(self.rdb)` with the null pointer. Redis dereferences it. The `TYPE_BLOB` branch in `read_buffer` already checks for a null handle, `load_chunk` didn't. Simplest way to hit it: ``` GRAPH.RESTORE x "" ``` While I was in there I also noticed the header, schema and payload directory decoders do `Vec::with_capacity(count as usize)` with counts read from the payload. A small payload with a huge count makes the process abort on the allocation. `GRAPH.BULK` already caps this kind of thing, so I did the same here. ## Changes - `load_chunk` returns an error if there is no IO handle - added `decode_capacity()` and used it for the pre-allocations in the header, schema and payload directory decoding - new flow test `tests/flow/test_graph_restore.py` (empty payload, truncated payload, wrong tag, huge counts), added to `flow_tests_done.txt` The RDB load path is not affected by the first change since it always has a real handle. ## Testing I don't have the full build set up locally (GraphBLAS / RediSearch), so I haven't run the flow tests myself and I'm relying on CI for that. Happy to fix anything it turns up. --- ## Summary by cubic `GRAPH.RESTORE` no longer crashes the server on empty, truncated, or malformed payloads; it returns an error instead. It also caps buffer pre-allocation sizes derived from payload counts to prevent process aborts from huge values. - `load_chunk` returns an error when there's no Redis IO handle instead of dereferencing null. - Count-based pre-allocations in header, schema, payload-directory, per-entity attributes, and `Value` arrays are capped at 1024 elements; vector dimensions are checked against buffer length. - Added flow tests for empty, truncated, wrong-tag, and oversized-count payloads, plus unit tests for the value and attribute decoders. Written for commit a1598bf77c98416f5f81f1b36db70f3c68b9ab2e. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Invalid or incomplete graph restore payloads are rejected with an error, while the server remains responsive and does not create a restored graph. * Decoding limits initial memory allocation for payload-specified counts, helping avoid excessive allocations when processing malformed data.

nodes.name: Cartesian product scans millions of targets before an empty index lookup
nodes.content:
# Cartesian product scans millions of targets before an empty index lookup

### Describe the situation

Hi, FalkorDB developers,

Please consider these two queries:

```cypher
// q1
MATCH (a:GspLow)
WHERE (a.id = 1)
MATCH (b:GspHigh)-[:GSP_LINK]->(c:GspTarget)
WHERE (c.keep = true)
RETURN a.uid, b.uid, c.uid;

// q2
MATCH (b:GspHigh)-[:GSP_LINK]->(c:GspTarget)
WHERE (c.keep = true)
MATCH (a:GspLow)
WHERE (a.id = 1)
RETURN a.uid, b.uid, c.uid;
```

I swap two independent `MATCH` clauses and get no rows from either query, because no `GspLow` node has `id=1`. In q1, FalkorDB stops after the empty index lookup. In q2, it scans 3,000,001 targets before checking the same index, and I measure about 236 times the runtime of q1.

### Which FalkorDB versions are affected?

I ran this case on FalkorDB 4.18.8, which reports module version `41808`, using Cypher in the FalkorDB Docker image on macOS ARM64.

### How to reproduce

Create this data in an empty graph, then run q1 and q2 above:

```cypher
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:GspLow) ON (n.id);

CREATE (:GspLow {uid: 1, id: 0}),
       (:GspHigh {uid: 2})-[:GSP_LINK]->(:GspTarget {uid: 3, keep: true});

UNWIND range(1, 750000) AS i
CREATE (b:GspHigh {uid: 895440+5*i})
WITH b, i
UNWIND range(1, 4) AS j
CREATE (b)-[:GSP_LINK]->(:GspTarget {uid: 895440+5*i+j, keep: false});
```

Wait until `CALL db.indexes()` reports the index as `OPERATIONAL`. The only `GspLow` node has `id=0`. The independent high branch has 3,000,001 targets, with only target 3 passing `c.keep=true`. None can contribute to the final result without a match for `a.id=1`.

For q1, I get no rows. Median runtime: **0.54 ms**.

For q2, I get no rows. Median runtime: **124.16 ms**.

Using `GRAPH.PROFILE` gives these excerpts from the native `Records produced` fields:

```text
q1:
Results | Records produced: 0
    Project | Records produced: 0
        Cartesian Product | Records produced: 0
            Node By Index Scan | (a:GspLow) | Records produced: 0
            Conditional Traverse | (c)->(b:GspHigh) | Records produced: 0
                Filter | Records produced: 0
                    Node By Label Scan | (c:GspTarget) | Records produced: 0

q2:
Results | Records produced: 0
    Project | Records produced: 0
        Cartesian Product | Records produced: 0
            Conditional Traverse | (b)->(b) | Records produced: 1
                Filter | Records produced: 1
                    Node By Label Scan | (c:GspTarget) | Records produced: 3000001
            Node By Index Scan | (a:GspLow) | Records produced: 0
```

For q2, FalkorDB scans the target label and checks `c.keep` before the Cartesian product reads the empty index result. For q1, it checks that index first and reads no target records, so the independent traversal contributes no work.

### Expected performance

Could FalkorDB check the small indexed input first in q2, as q1 does, so the Cartesian product can stop without scanning the independent target branch when the lookup returns no rows?

nodes.name: Repeated traversal after swapping independent OPTIONAL MATCH clauses
nodes.content:
# Repeated traversal after swapping independent OPTIONAL MATCH clauses

### Describe the situation

Hi, FalkorDB developers,

Please consider these two queries:

```cypher
// q1
MATCH (u:GspAnchor)
OPTIONAL MATCH (u)-[:GSP_LOW]->(v:GspLow)
OPTIONAL MATCH (u)-[:GSP_HIGH]->(w:GspHigh)
WHERE (w.keep = true)
RETURN u.uid, v.uid, w.uid;

// q2
MATCH (u:GspAnchor)
OPTIONAL MATCH (u)-[:GSP_HIGH]->(w:GspHigh)
WHERE (w.keep = true)
OPTIONAL MATCH (u)-[:GSP_LOW]->(v:GspLow)
RETURN u.uid, v.uid, w.uid;
```

I swap two `OPTIONAL MATCH` clauses that share only `u`; the condition uses only `w`. Both queries return the same ten rows, including the rows with a missing low or high neighbor. For q1, FalkorDB repeats the high traversal for each low neighbor, and I measure about eight times the runtime of q2.

### Which FalkorDB versions are affected?

I ran this case on FalkorDB 4.18.8, which reports module version `41808`, using Cypher in the FalkorDB Docker image on macOS ARM64.

### How to reproduce

Create this data in an empty graph, then run q1 and q2 above:

```cypher
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:GspAnchor) ON (n.uid);

CREATE (a:GspAnchor {uid: 1})-[:GSP_LOW]->(:GspLow {uid: 10})
CREATE (a)-[:GSP_HIGH]->(:GspHigh {uid: 20, keep: true})
CREATE (:GspAnchor {uid: 2})-[:GSP_LOW]->(:GspLow {uid: 11})
CREATE (:GspAnchor {uid: 3})-[:GSP_HIGH]->(:GspHigh {uid: 21, keep: true});

MATCH (u:GspAnchor {uid: 1})
UNWIND range(1, 400000) AS i
CREATE (u)-[:GSP_HIGH]->(:GspHigh {uid: 895440+i, keep: false});

MATCH (u:GspAnchor {uid: 1})
UNWIND range(1, 7) AS i
CREATE (u)-[:GSP_LOW]->(:GspLow {uid: -i});
```

Wait until `CALL db.indexes()` reports the index as `OPERATIONAL`. Anchor 1 has eight low neighbors and 400,001 high neighbors, with only high neighbor 20 passing `keep=true`. Anchor 2 has a low neighbor and no high neighbor; anchor 3 has a high neighbor and no low neighbor.

For q1, I get ten rows in columns `(u.uid, v.uid, w.uid)`: `(1, 10, 20)`, `(1, -1, 20)`, `(1, -2, 20)`, `(1, -3, 20)`, `(1, -4, 20)`, `(1, -5, 20)`, `(1, -6, 20)`, `(1, -7, 20)`, `(2, 11, null)` and `(3, null, 21)`. Median runtime: **186.11 ms**.

For q2, I get the same ten rows. Median runtime: **23.55 ms**.

Using `GRAPH.PROFILE` gives these excerpts from the native `Records produced` fields:

```text
q1:
Results | Records produced: 10
    Project | Records produced: 10
        Apply | Records produced: 10
            Optional Conditional Traverse | (u)->(v:GspLow) | Records produced: 10
                Node By Label Scan | (u:GspAnchor) | Records produced: 3
            Optional | Records produced: 10
                Filter | Records produced: 9
                    Conditional Traverse | (u)->(w:GspHigh) | Records produced: 3200009
                        Argument | Records produced: 10

q2:
Results | Records produced: 10
    Project | Records produced: 10
        Optional Conditional Traverse | (u)->(v:GspLow) | Records produced: 10
            Apply | Records produced: 3
                Node By Label Scan | (u:GspAnchor) | Records produced: 3
                Optional | Records produced: 3
                    Filter | Records produced: 2
                        Conditional Traverse | (u)->(w:GspHigh) | Records produced: 400002
                            Argument | Records produced: 3
```


### Expected performance

Could FalkorDB avoid repeating an optional traversal that depends only on `u` by evaluating and filtering it before multiplying the low-neighbor matches, as q2 does?

nodes.name: fix(index): release open index scans before commit; read the pending count without the mutex
nodes.content:
Fixes #3226

## What this PR does

Two fixes for lock hazards around the indexes that RediSearch backs.

- Before a query takes the GIL to commit, it reads every RediSearch query that it still has open to the end and frees it. The scan then yields the buffered rest as before. `LIMIT` also drops its input once the limit is met, so a `LIMIT k` write frees its scan before the commit and buffers nothing.
- `Index::pending_count` reads an atomic copy of the current-generation pending count. A BGSAVE child then never takes the pending-slots mutex.

This applies to the default build. Queries that hold no open index scan at commit time do not change. Of the pending-slot functions, only the readers of `pending_count` change: the RDB encoder, `CALL db.indexes()` and the planner's index checks.

## Why we need this

On `main`, a write query whose index scan is still open at commit time stops the server or aborts it. Two common shapes keep a scan open: an index scan below `LIMIT`, and an index scan that feeds a `CALL {}` subquery.

- The server stops answering when another client runs a command that needs the RediSearch write lock under the GIL. `RESTORE` of a graph with indexes is one such command. The writer holds the RediSearch read locks and waits for the GIL. The GIL holder waits for the RediSearch write lock.
- The server aborts when the query writes the property that its scan reads. The index write fails the assertion `attempted to upgrade a spec read lock to a write lock`.

A BGSAVE child can also block forever on the pending-slots mutex of an index. BGSAVE then never finishes, and a replica that needs a full sync waits for it. Each later BGSAVE fails with `Background save already in progress`. The window is short, so the hang is rare. When it occurs, nothing recovers from it without a restart.

## Root cause: open index scans at commit

Line numbers are for `main` at `ec2448f`, with `deps/RediSearch` at `ea1a6f4`.

- An open RediSearch iterator holds two read locks. `handleIterCommon` takes the global `RWLOCK` read lock and the spec read lock (`deps/RediSearch/src/redisearch_api.c:904-905`). Only `RediSearch_ResultsIteratorFree` releases them (`:1045`).
- `IndexResultsIter` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:268`), `EdgeTripleIter` (`:355`) and `ScoredEdgeTripleIter` (`:419`) free the iterator only in `Drop` (`:336`, `:406`, `:472`).
- `LimitOp::next` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/limit.rs:49`) keeps its child after the limit is met (`:72`, `:83`). The scan below stays open until the query ends.
- A `CALL {}` subquery commits once per input batch while the outer scan is still open.
- `CommitOp` commits the pending changes (`graph/src/runtime/ops/commit.rs:89`). It then takes the GIL in `upgrade_to_write` (`:96`, `src/query_session.rs:221`, `escalate` at `:242`). Last, it writes the deferred index changes (`commit.rs:103`).
- `IndexSpec_LockWrite` finds the read lock of the same thread on that spec and aborts (`deps/RediSearch/src/spec.c:2304`).

## Root cause: pending count in the BGSAVE child

- The RDB encoder runs in the BGSAVE child. `Schema::from_graph` (`src/serializers/mod.rs:708`) calls `Indexer::index_info` (`graph/src/index/indexer.rs:793`), which reads `pending_count` of every index (`:805`).
- `Index::pending_count` locks `pending_slots`, a `parking_lot::Mutex` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:2164`).
- Other threads take that mutex all the time. Population workers take it for every ticket (`increment_pending_for_generation` at `:2110`, `try_decrement_pending_for_generation` at `:2128`). Query threads take it when the planner checks an index (`graph/src/index/indexer.rs:445`, `:459`).
- `fork` copies only the calling thread. A mutex that another thread holds at that moment stays locked in the child, and no thread can release it.

The code already states the intent. `index_info` says "Lock-free snapshot: safe to call from a BGSAVE fork child" (`indexer.rs:794-795`). `graph_rdb_save` bypasses the graph `RwLock` for the same reason (`src/redis_type.rs:190-191`).

## The fix

Open index scans:

- Every RediSearch iterator is now an `OpenQuery` behind `Rc<RefCell<..>>`. A weak reference to it goes into the thread-local list `OPEN_QUERIES`.
- `release_open_queries()` reads each open query of the calling thread to its end, buffers the rest of its results and frees the C iterator. The iterator then yields from the buffer.
- A query that reaches its end frees its C iterator at once, not when the operator tree drops it.
- `QuerySession::upgrade_to_write` calls `release_open_queries()` on every call, before it takes the GIL. A writer can open new scans between two commits, and an inline session starts as a writer.
- `abandon_write` calls it before the index resync, which also writes the index.
- `LimitOp` replaces its child with an empty op once the limit is met. The child is never pulled again, and a `CALL {}` subquery builds a new op tree for each input batch.

Pending count:

- `Index` gets `current_pending: Arc<AtomicI32>`. Clones of the `Index` share it, as they share `pending_slots`.
- `bump_id`, `increment_pending_for_generation` and `try_decrement_pending_for_generation` store the new current-generation count into it while they hold the mutex.
- `pending_count` loads it with `Ordering::Relaxed` and takes no lock. The count is a status value, and no reader orders other memory accesses on it.

## Tests

- New flow test `test_index_updates.py::test13_write_to_index_scanned_under_limit`. It writes the scanned property under `LIMIT 10`, then in a `CALL {}` subquery over 2,000 rows. It checks the returned counts and the indexed values. On stock `main`, the server aborts at the first query of the new test.
- The pending count has no new flow test. A test would need a fork at the instant another thread holds the mutex, which a flow test cannot arrange.
- The flow set below ran in services mode, with a replica for the files that need one. Stock `main` passed 515 of 515 tests. With both fixes, this branch passed 516 of 516.
- `test_effects_ddl.py::testEffects_06_ConstraintSettlingRaces::test02` is a known flake that the file documents. In three reruns of that file, the open-scan fix alone passed 3 of 3. Stock `main` failed 2 of 3 with the same assertion.

With a replica: `test_constraint`, `test_ro_query`, `test_replication`, `test_effects_commit`, `test_effects_ddl`, `test_persistency`, `test_graph_deletion`, `test_rdb_load`, `test_stress`, `test_graph_copy`, `test_memory_usage`, `test_pause_replication_race`, `test_replication_states`.

nodes.name: perf(constraint): look UNIQUE keys up in the supporting index
nodes.content:
## What this PR does

UNIQUE enforcement looks the keys of a commit up in the constraint's supporting range index. It no longer scans the label once per affected entity. The second commit checks only the entities whose key or membership the commit can change.

This applies to every commit that touches an entity under a UNIQUE constraint. MANDATORY constraints do not change.

Fixes #2995. It is an alternative to #2997, and keeps the one-pass check of #2997 as its fallback.

## Why we need this

On `main`, a UNIQUE check costs one pass over the whole label per affected entity (#2995). A write of one entity costs O(label size). A batch of k rows costs O(k x label size).

- One `CREATE` takes 20.9 ms at 100,000 nodes and 0.76 ms at 1,000 nodes.
- A `SET` of an unconstrained property costs the same, because every touched entity is checked.
- Loading 30,000 nodes in three 10,000-row queries takes 111 s.

## Merge order

The index lookup is exact only while the index holds every entity with its current values. Two open bugs break that on `main`, so this PR depends on #3086 and #3098:

- #3069, fixed by #3086: a field added to an index during its population stays empty while the index reports OPERATIONAL.
- #3095, fixed by #3098: a population batch can overwrite a newer document or add a deleted entity back.

Without them, a lookup can miss an existing key, and a duplicate gets in. `test_effects_ddl.py::testEffects_06_ConstraintSettlingRaces::test01` shows it: it fails on this PR alone and passes with #3086 and #3098 under it. Merge this PR after both.

## Root cause

Line numbers are for `main` at `ec2448f`.

- `Pending::enforce_constraints` (`graph/src/runtime/pending.rs:1258`) calls `check_node_constraint` (`:1355`) and `check_edge_constraint` (`:1425`).
- For each affected entity, `check_node_constraint` builds a map of the composite keys of the whole label (`:1397`, loop at `:1400`). `check_edge_constraint` does the same per relationship type (`:1470`, loop at `:1473`).
- The check runs for every touched entity, including entities whose constrained properties the commit did not change.

## The fix

- The commit keys every entity it checks into one map. Two entities of the commit with one key fail at once.
- The other entities are looked up in the supporting range index, 1,024 keys per RediSearch query. The query is a union of rows, and each row is an intersection of one exact match per property.
- Each hit is read back from the graph and compared by the same composite key. A hit that matches only as `f64` does not count. Neither does the stale document of an entity that this commit changed, deleted or unlabelled.
- The lookup runs only while the index is OPERATIONAL, and only for values that the index stores exactly. These are booleans, integers up to 2^53, finite floats, and non-empty strings below the 4,096-byte tag limit.
- In every other case, one pass over the label checks all keys of the commit at once, as #2997 does. The pass also runs when a commit carries more keys than a quarter of the graph's entities.
- Debug builds run both checks and assert that they agree.
- The second commit skips the UNIQUE check for an entity whose key cannot change. A new duplicate needs at least one entity that the commit created, gave the label, or set a constrained property on.

## Behavior change

- A duplicate pair that already exists no longer fails an unrelated `SET` on one of its entities. Such a pair can exist when two equal keys are written while the constraint is still validating.
- A `SET` of a constrained property is still checked against every other member, with the full composite key. A swap is judged by the full keys of both entities.
- C FalkorDB and #2997 still reject that unrelated `SET`.

## Tests

New flow tests, class `testUniqueConstraintIndexLookup` in `tests/flow/test_constraint.py`:

- `test01_bulk_load`: 20,000 nodes in one query under UNIQUE, within 10 s. Stock `main` fails it: 47.97 s.
- `test02_node_duplicates`: duplicates of an existing node, within one query, by `SET`, by `MERGE`, by a new label. It checks 1, 500 and 10,000 keys, which covers the lookup and the label pass. Swaps, reuse of a freed value in one query, and `'10'` against `10` must pass.
- `test03_edge_duplicates`: the same cases for relationships.
- `test04_partial_composite_change`: a `SET` of one property of a composite key is judged by the whole key.

Flow set of 34 files, services mode, with a replica for the files that need one:

| Build | Passed | Failed |
|---|---|---|
| Stock `main` | 515 of 515 | none |
| This PR alone | 518 of 519 | `test_effects_ddl` class 06 `test01`: "a duplicate must be rejected" |
| This PR on #3086 and #3098 | 521 of 521 | none |
| The same, debug assertions on | 521 of 521 | none; the lookup and the label pass agreed on every check |
| The same, plus the open-scan PR | 522 of 522 | none |

## Measurements

Write latency on a label of 1k, 10k, 30k and 100k nodes with UNIQUE `(id)`. The nodes were loaded first, then the index and the constraint were created. Medians of 30 single writes and of 5 batches, in ms:

| Write | Stock `main` | This PR | This PR on #3086 and #3098 |
|---|---|---|---|
| One `CREATE` | 0.76, 2.16, 4.93, 20.9 | 0.41, 0.33, 0.38, 0.29 | 0.39, 0.28, 0.33, 0.29 |
| `MATCH` by id, then `SET` of another property | 0.48, 1.86, 4.84, 19.5 | 0.33, 0.18, 0.21, 0.29 | 0.26, 0.25, 0.22, 0.37 |
| One `UNWIND` of 100 `CREATE` | 17.3, 155, 469, 1,850 | 0.48, 0.47, 0.75, 0.66 | 0.71, 0.64, 0.48, 0.57 |

The same writes, with the constraint created before the load of 10k-row queries. Stock `main` timed out on the 100k load: one 10k-row query ran over 120 s. The cells for the patched builds give the median of 3 runs:

| Write | Stock `main` | This PR | This PR on #3086 and #3098 |
|---|---|---|---|
| One `CREATE` | 0.69, 2.03, 6.36, timed out | 0.42, 0.34, 0.38, 0.38 | 0.42, 0.49, 0.44, 0.33 |
| `MATCH` by id, then `SET` of another property | 0.45, 1.92, 6.00, timed out | 0.26, 0.36, 0.29, 0.25 | 0.31, 0.33, 0.40, 0.25 |
| One `UNWIND` of 100 `CREATE` | 18.4, 140, 476, timed out | 0.77, 0.58, 0.71, 0.58 | 0.60, 0.66, 0.79, 0.72 |

Without a constraint, stock `main` takes 0.24 to 0.37 ms for one `CREATE` at every size.

Bulk load under UNIQUE, in 10k-row queries:

| Nodes | Stock `main` | This PR | This PR on #3086 and #3098 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30,000 | 111 s: 16.8, 34.0 and 60.3 s per query | 0.08 s | 0.06 s |
| 100,000 | not run | 0.26 s | 0.21 s |

A `CALL {}` subquery sets `n.y` on each row of an index scan. A second client runs `RESTORE` every 100 ms, and a third sends PING every 20 ms. Both builds carry the open-scan PR (`fix/index-scan-read-locks-across-commit`): without it, this shape deadlocks against `RESTORE` on `main`. Two runs of 15 s each:

| Scan | `main` with the open-scan PR | The same, plus #3086, #3098 and this PR |

| 3,000 nodes, UNIQUE on the scanned key: CALL p50; PING p99 | 1,038 and 1,084 ms; 1,196 and 1,214 ms | 9.2 and 12.0 ms; 13.0 and 16.8 ms |
| 20,000 nodes, UNIQUE | the query times out at 30 s; one PING waits 30.0 s | 63 and 84 ms; 63 and 143 ms |
| 20,000 nodes, no constraint, for reference | 49 and 76 ms; 41 and 99 ms | 66 and 71 ms; 58 and 93 ms |

nodes.name: fix(index): read the pending count without the pending-slots mutex
nodes.content: ## What this PR does `Index::pending_count` now reads an atomic copy of the current-generation pending count. Every change of that count under the pending-slots mutex also stores it in the atomic. The other pending-slot functions do not change. This applies to every build. Only the readers of `pending_count` change: the RDB encoder, `CALL db.indexes()` and the planner's index checks. ## Why we need this A BGSAVE child can block forever on the pending-slots mutex of an index. BGSAVE then never finishes, and a replica that needs a full sync waits for it. Each later BGSAVE fails with `Background save already in progress`. The hang needs a fork while another thread holds the mutex. That window is short, so the hang is rare. When it occurs, nothing recovers from it without a restart. ## Root cause Line numbers are for `main` at `ec2448f`. - The RDB encoder runs in the BGSAVE child. `Schema::from_graph` (`src/serializers/mod.rs:708`) calls `Indexer::index_info` (`graph/src/index/indexer.rs:793`), which reads `pending_count` of every index (`:805`). - `Index::pending_count` locks `pending_slots`, a `parking_lot::Mutex` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:2164`). - Other threads take that mutex all the time. Population workers take it for every ticket (`increment_pending_for_generation` at `:2110`, `try_decrement_pending_for_generation` at `:2128`). Query threads take it when the planner checks an index (`graph/src/index/indexer.rs:445`, `:459`). - `fork` copies only the calling thread. A mutex that another thread holds at that moment stays locked in the child, and no thread can release it. The code already states the intent. `index_info` says "Lock-free snapshot: safe to call from a BGSAVE fork child" (`indexer.rs:794-795`). `graph_rdb_save` bypasses the graph `RwLock` for the same reason (`src/redis_type.rs:190-191`). ## The fix - `Index` gets `current_pending: Arc`. Clones of the `Index` share it, as they share `pending_slots`. - `bump_id`, `increment_pending_for_generation` and `try_decrement_pending_for_generation` store the new current-generation count into it while they hold the mutex. - `pending_count` loads it with `Ordering::Relaxed` and takes no lock. The count is a status value, and no reader orders other memory accesses on it. ## Tests - No new flow test. A test would need a fork at the instant another thread holds the mutex, which a flow test cannot arrange. - The flow set of 34 files ran in services mode, with a replica for the files that need one. Stock `main` and this branch both passed 515 of 515 tests. ## Measurements | Check | Stock `main` | This PR | |---|---|---| | BGSAVE while one thread holds the pending-slots mutex (fault injection, below) | the child blocks in `futex_wait`; `rdb_bgsave_in_progress:1` after 30 s | BGSAVE finishes at once | | 2,600 BGSAVE runs while 8 clients loop `CALL db.indexes()` on 64 or 256 indexes | 2,600 of 2,600 finish | not run | - The second row shows that load alone rarely opens the window. Each BGSAVE child finished on stock `main`. - In the first row, the stock child has this stack: `RawMutex::lock_slow`, `Indexer::index_info`, `Graph::index_info`, `encode_graph`, `rdb_save_graph_key`, `graph_rdb_save`, `rdbSaveObject`, then Redis's `rdbSaveBackground`. Environment: Apple silicon, Docker linux/arm64 VM with 15 CPUs. Release `falkordb.so` from each branch, built with the builder stage of `build/runtime/Dockerfile`, in the `falkordb/falkordb:6.0.2` image (Redis 8.10.2). The first row ran with the default module arguments. The second row ran with `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT 30000 TIMEOUT_MAX 60000 RESULTSET_SIZE -1 MAX_QUEUED_QUERIES 200 NODE_CREATION_BUFFER 1024 CACHE_SIZE 10 QUERY_MEM_CAPACITY 268435456 ASYNC_DELETE no THREAD_COUNT 4`: 2,300 runs on all CPUs and 300 runs pinned to one CPU. ## Repro: setup A fork has to land while another thread holds the mutex. This repro makes that certain: it patches one instruction of the running server, so that a population worker spins inside the mutex. The patch runs as root in a sidecar container that shares the server's PID namespace and has `SYS_PTRACE`. On the arm64 build of `ec2448f`, the first instruction after the lock in `Indexer::release_population_ticket` is at offset `0x38c188`: `ldr x8, [x21, #24]`, bytes `a8 0e 40 f9`. On this branch it is at `0x38c1a8`. ## Repro: procedure 1. Find the offset for your `falkordb.so` with `objdump -d`: the first instruction after the lock in `Indexer::release_population_ticket`. 2. Run `redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(1, 100) AS i CREATE (:P {v: i})"`. 3. Run the script below with the server's PID and the offset. It writes `b .` (`00 00 00 14`) over that instruction through `/proc//mem`. 4. Run `redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:P) ON (n.v)"`. The population worker spins at the patched instruction with the mutex held. 5. Run `redis-cli BGSAVE`, then `redis-cli INFO persistence` every few seconds. On stock `main`, `rdb_bgsave_in_progress` stays at `1`. With this PR it returns to `0` at once. ```python import sys off = int(sys.argv[2], 16) base = None for line in open(f"/proc/{sys.argv[1]}/maps"): f = line.split() if len(f) >= 6 and f[5].endswith("/falkordb.so") and int(f[2], 16) == 0: base = int(f[0].split("-")[0], 16) break with open(f"/proc/{sys.argv[1]}/mem", "r+b", buffering=0) as mem: mem.seek(base + off) assert mem.read(4) == bytes.fromhex("a80e40f9") mem.seek(base + off) mem.write(bytes.fromhex("00000014")) ``` ## Repro with a debugger On a debug build, a debugger in non-stop mode does the same job. Stop the population thread on a line inside `try_decrement_pending_for_generation`, after the lock. Run BGSAVE while the thread is stopped. --- ## Summary by cubic Prevents a BGSAVE child from hanging forever by making `Index::pending_count` read an atomic copy of the pending count instead of taking the pending-slots mutex. The count is stored in an `Arc` whenever it changes under the mutex; `pending_count` now loads it with relaxed ordering and does not lock. Since `fork` copies only the calling thread, a child can inherit a mutex that remains locked forever; this removes that failure mode from BGSAVE and any other reader of the pending count. Written for commit c3ec97513fd6be9f4383eb21d8be3d6d2da81dd4. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Performance** * Checking the current amount of pending work now avoids waiting for a bookkeeping lock, which can reduce coordination overhead during index updates. Generation-specific counts and handling of work from older generations remain unchanged, preserving existing count behavior while making this common check more efficient.

nodes.name: Write with an open index scan aborts or stalls the server; BGSAVE child can block on the pending-slots mutex
nodes.content:
## Summary

On `main` at `ec2448f`, two lock hazards in the indexes that RediSearch backs can stop the server.

- A write query that still has an index scan open when it commits aborts the server. With a `RESTORE` running beside it, the server stops answering instead.
- A BGSAVE child can block forever on the pending-slots mutex of an index.

## 1. A write commits while its index scan is open

Two common query shapes keep a scan open at commit time: an index scan below `LIMIT`, and an index scan that feeds a `CALL {}` subquery.

Repro on a stock `main` server. The last command aborts the server:

```
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(1, 2000) AS i CREATE (:W {v: i})"
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:W) ON (n.v)"
# wait until this prints OPERATIONAL
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "CALL db.indexes() YIELD status RETURN status"
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:W) WHERE n.v > 0 WITH n LIMIT 10 SET n.v = n.v + 100000 RETURN count(n)"
```

- Expected: the query returns 10.
- Actual: the server aborts, and the log shows `attempted to upgrade a spec read lock to a write lock`.

The stall needs two clients. Client A loops `MATCH (n:D) WHERE n.id > 0 WITH n LIMIT 5 SET n.x = n.x + 1` over 20,000 nodes with a range index on `:D(id)`. Client B loops `GRAPH.DELETE r` and `RESTORE r` of a 2,000-node graph with one range index.

- Expected: both loops make progress, and PING answers.
- Actual: PING gets no reply after 0.2 s, and neither loop completes another command. The writer holds the RediSearch read locks and waits for the GIL. The `RESTORE` holds the GIL and waits for the RediSearch write lock.

## 2. A BGSAVE child blocks on the pending-slots mutex

The RDB encoder runs in the BGSAVE child. It calls `Indexer::index_info`, which reads `Index::pending_count` of every index. `pending_count` locks the `pending_slots` mutex (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:2164`). Population workers and query threads take that mutex often. If another thread holds it at the fork, no thread in the child can release it.

- Expected: BGSAVE finishes.
- Actual: the child blocks forever, and `rdb_bgsave_in_progress` stays at `1`. A replica that needs a full sync waits for it. Each later BGSAVE fails with `Background save already in progress`.

The window is short, so load alone rarely hits it. To force it, stop a population worker after the lock in `try_decrement_pending_for_generation`, for example with a debugger in non-stop mode. Then run `BGSAVE`.

The blocked child has this stack: `RawMutex::lock_slow`, `Indexer::index_info`, `Graph::index_info`, `encode_graph`, `rdb_save_graph_key`, `graph_rdb_save`, `rdbSaveObject`, `rdbSaveBackground`.

## Version

`main` at `ec2448f` with `deps/RediSearch` at `ea1a6f4`, in the `falkordb/falkordb:6.0.2` runtime image (Redis 8.10.2), linux/arm64.

A fix for both is in #3223.

nodes.content:
# FalkorDB v6.0.2

## What's Changed

### Bug fixes
* CALL {} subqueries that import no variables no longer read the outer query's variables (#2845)
* Variable-length and allShortestPaths patterns apply an inline property map on an already-bound endpoint; inline maps are planned once instead of twice (#2390)
* Range index scans include ±inf for an open bound and return undirected edges in both directions (#3081)
* Temporals are no longer matched by numeric range-index predicates (#3076)
* An exclusive string range with equal bounds selects nothing (#3072)
* A wrong-dimension vector no longer drops the entity from every index on its label (#3087)
* Vector KNN queries clamp `k` instead of allocating `k` entries (#3088)
* Validate index OPTIONS like 4.x: vector `dimension`/`similarityFunction` required, case-insensitive metric, unknown fulltext keys rejected (#3094)
* Parser: reject `NOT NOT`, `SET [n)`, `f(1,)`, `MATCH MATCH`, `LOAD CSV WITH`; accept `IS NULL IN` (#3060)
* Block comments end at `*/`, and a lone `/` is no longer swallowed (#2908)
* Named paths created by CREATE are materialized (#2829)
* `startNode()` and `endNode()` accept null (#3132)
* Compact date and time strings with non-digits are rejected (#3125)
* `toInteger` of an integer string below i64::MIN returns null (#2989)
* `sign()` of a float returns an integer (#2907)
* `coalesce()` with zero arguments is rejected (#2990)
* `list.remove` with a huge count no longer overflows (#2952)
* Type-mismatch errors name types as Cypher does (#3127)
* UDF results keep -0.0, constructor-keyed maps and non-finite vecf32 (#3074)
* The `graph` global is defined when a UDF library is loaded (#3079)
* One flag parser for GRAPH.QUERY/RO_QUERY/PROFILE/EXPLAIN, matching 4.x (#3010)
* GRAPH.CONFIG validates values, arity and names like 4.x (#3021)
* GRAPH.MEMORY accepts `SAMPLES 0`; GRAPH.CONSTRAINT parses entity type and count like 4.x (#3053)
* RDBs keep every graph in GRAPH.LIST when loaded by 4.x (#3161)
* GRAPH.EFFECT refuses records that act on deleted or never-created entities (#3022)
* GRAPH.EFFECT refuses ids too large for any graph instead of crashing (#2911)
* Effects encoder refuses records its reader would reject (#2916)
* Decoded effect id lists keep their order when extended (#2920)

### Improvements
* IdSpace is the single authority for node and relationship ids; writes run the same id check as replicas (#2846)
* CoW B+-tree: point lookups, memory accounting, tuple cursor, narrowable doc width (#2278)

### Build & CI
* Docker: redis-server runs as the non-root `falkordb` user; set `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1` to keep root (#3181)
* Docker: remove util-linux from the runtime image; add a Trivy image scan to CI (#3179)
* Replace graphblas.sh/redisearch.sh with a `native-deps` crate; GraphBLAS and LAGraph are now submodules (#2695)
* Move the toolchain to LLVM 23 (#3163)
* Fix the RediSearch build with libc++ 23 on macOS (#3170)

### Dependencies
* rustls 0.23.41 → 0.23.45 (#3182)
* cargo-deps group, 9 updates (#3131)
* github-actions group, 6 updates (#2886)
* rltest >= 0.7.29 (#3130)

### Tests
* Cover OPTIONAL MATCH cartesian product cardinality (#2469), fixed-length path multiplicity (#2471), crash-inducing `range()`/`exists()` arguments (#2487), nested reduce with shadowed names (#2488), and aggregating `WITH *` in allShortestPaths (#2489)

Thanks to @onlyysaurabh, @aniruddhaadak80 and @juliuskent11 for their contributions.

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/compare/v6.0.1...v6.0.2

✨ New features

Advanced path-finding algorithms (#2630, #2720, #2656, #2732)
- A* search with an admissible haversine heuristic + optional heuristicScale so it stays optimal for non-distance weights like travel time (heuristicScale = 1/max_speed; 0 = Dijkstra). Fixes ~1.6× suboptimal routes on time-weighted road networks.
- Yen's k-shortest paths with goal-directed spur search.
- All-shortest-paths and k-shortest-paths procedures.
- Optimality/cost-model fixes: correct pathCost/hop-count accounting, cost-aware k-shortest selection, redundant destination-lookup skip in landmark mode.

CCH path index (#2680, #2721, #2865)
- DDL: CREATE CCH INDEX FOR ()-[e:A|B]->() ON (e.w) / DROP CCH INDEX …. Multi-reltype supported; hierarchy stays internal (no shortcut edges / rank props in your graph).
- Query: db.idx.cch.query — rank-pruned bidirectional Dijkstra.
- Incremental maintenance: commit-coalesced dirty tracking (CLEAN < RECUSTOMIZE < REBUILD); weight/edge changes recustomize scoped, topology changes rebuild.
- Persistence: full RDB serialization, restored on load.

🐛 Bug fixes

- Crash on MERGE preceded by an erroring clause (#3116).
- Crash when a clause errors mid plan-build (#3139).
- Replica SIGSEGV applying an UPDATE_EDGE/UPDATE_NODE effect naming a freed id (id divergence) (#2581).

🔄 Replication & persistence

nodes.name: FalkorDB/FalkorDB v6.0.0
nodes.content:
# FalkorDB 6.0.0

FalkorDB 6.0 is the first release of the new FalkorDB engine, written in Rust. It replaces the C engine that shipped in every 4.x release.

For applications nothing changes: it is still a Redis module named `graph`, with the same `GRAPH.*` commands, the same Cypher, and the same client libraries. What changes is how replication works and which packages are published. Read **Upgrading from 4.x** before moving a production deployment.

## Upgrading from 4.x

### Replication
**Don't mix 4.x and 6.0 in the same primary/replica set.** 6.0 replicates writes only as effects in a new format, v3 (#2570, #2754), which 4.x can't read, and 6.0 can't apply the effects 4.x sends. Upgrade every node in a replication group together.

### Configuration
- `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD` is accepted but ignored: effects are now the only replication mechanism. `GRAPH.CONFIG GET` still returns the value you set, so existing config files keep working.
- `TIMEOUT` stays deprecated, as in 4.x. Use `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` and `TIMEOUT_MAX`.

## Packages

**Docker.** `falkordb/falkordb` and `falkordb/falkordb-server` on Docker Hub and GHCR:

| Tag | Now points at |
|---|---|
| `6.0.0`, `latest` | 6.0 (Rust engine), amd64 + arm64 |
| `edge` | the latest `main` build (Rust engine); `edge-rs` is a deprecated alias |
| `v4.x.y`, `edge-c` | the C engine, unchanged |
| `latest-alpine`, `*-alpine` | still the C engine (4.20.7). 6.0 has no Alpine images. |

The `falkordb/falkordb` image bundles FalkorDB Browser on port 3000, as before.

**Module binaries** attached to this release, with `SHA256SUMS`:

| Asset | Platform |
|---|---|
| `falkordb-x64.so` | Linux x86-64 |
| `falkordb-arm64v8.so` | Linux arm64 |
| `falkordb-rhel9-x64.so` | RHEL 9 x86-64 |
| `falkordb-amazonlinux2023-x64.so` | Amazon Linux 2023 x86-64 |

4.20 also published Alpine, RHEL 8, macOS and `debug-*` builds. 6.0 does not publish those yet.

## What's different from 4.20.7

- **New engine.** The query engine is new code, written in Rust. Your queries and clients carry over: the `GRAPH.*` commands and Cypher are the same.
- **Replicas apply changes, they don't re-run queries.** 4.x sent some writes to replicas as the query text, and the replica ran the query again. 6.0 always sends the resulting changes, so a replica never re-executes a write. `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD`, which chose between the two, is now ignored.
- **Newer search engine.** Full-text and vector indexes run on RediSearch 8.6.1, up from 2.6.23. Full-text scoring still defaults to TFIDF, so scores match 4.x.
- **`GRAPH.BULK` no longer reserves memory from the counts a client declares up front,** so a wrong or malicious count can't exhaust the server's memory (#2444).
- **Same Redis.** 6.0 is built on Redis 8.10.2, as is 4.20.7.

## Not in 6.0 yet

**Algorithms.** 6.0 has the same procedures as 4.20.7, and you lose nothing by upgrading. These algorithms were developed for the C engine after 4.20 and have not shipped in any release. They are being ported to the new engine:
- **A\* shortest paths** (`algo.AStar`), guided by latitude/longitude, with a k-shortest-paths variant (#2947).
- **Customizable Contraction Hierarchies** (`algo.CCH`, `algo.CCH.query`), for fast repeated shortest-path queries (#2948).
- **Leiden and Louvain community detection** (`algo.leiden`, `algo.louvain`), still in development (#2949).

**Packages.** 6.0 publishes no Alpine images, and no Alpine, RHEL 8, macOS or `debug-*` module builds (see Packages). `latest-alpine` stays on 4.20.7.

**Mixed-engine replication.** A 4.x node and a 6.0 node can't replicate to each other (see Upgrading from 4.x).

## If you ran the preview images (`edge`, `edge-rs`)

The new engine has been available as a preview since August. Changes since then:

- **Faster queries,** especially filters and label checks, multi-hop traversals, queries with many parameters, aggregations, and deleting nodes.
- **Less memory** on write-heavy workloads.
- **Crash and hang fixes:** very deeply nested expressions, nested index scans, pattern comprehensions, `algo.SPpaths` on large graphs, and shutdown under heavy telemetry.
- **Wrong-result fixes** around `NULL` (joins, `CASE`, composite `UNIQUE` constraints), a label removed and re-added in one query, and deleting an edge created earlier in the same query.
- **Closer to 4.x behaviour:** `GRAPH.INFO` output, NUL bytes in queries, and `INFO` no longer showing RediSearch's version as FalkorDB's (#2915).
- **Docker image fixes:** the bundled Browser starts, and `redis-sentinel`, `redis-check-rdb` and `redis-check-aof` are back.

The full list is in the pull requests merged into `main` since #2279.

nodes.name: FalkorDB/FalkorDB v4.20.7
nodes.content:
Patch release on top of v4.20.6. Contains a security update, two bug fixes, and a CI change.

Full changelog: v4.20.6...v4.20.7

🔒 Security

- Bump Redis to 8.10.2 for CVE-2026-85091. Updates the pinned Redis version across all Docker images (build + server) and the sanitizer/test paths. (#2850, fixes #2849)

🐛 Bug Fixes

- Prevent crash from concurrent GRAPH.CONSTRAINT creation. A write query reserves node IDs under the read lock, then releases it to commit under the write lock; in that gap a failing async GRAPH.CONSTRAINT could roll back and zero the graph-global reserved_node_count, driving it negative on the write query's commit — an assert in debug and datablock corruption (later crash) in release. A read-locked pre-check now rejects the common benign failures (constraint already exists, missing supporting index, duplicate properties) without taking the write lock or rolling back. (#2875, fixes #2880; partially mitigates the underflow crash tracked in #238 — a TOCTOU residual remains)
- Seek-by-id now optimizes compound expressions opposite ID(n). Filters like ID(a) = x + 1, ID(b) = ID(a) + 1, reversed operands, inequalities, and multi-bound ranges now reduce a scan+filter to a NodeByIdSeek (previously only bare operands qualified). Also fixes a correctness bug where a per-record bound resolving to an empty range (non-integer / out-of-range value) dropped all remaining records instead of skipping just that one — e.g. UNWIND [1.1, 2, 3.5, 4] AS x MATCH (n) WHERE ID(n) = x now returns nodes 2 and 4. (#2870, fixes #2871)

nodes.name: Paths whose contents EXECUTE with this repository's credentials, rather than
nodes.content:
# Paths whose contents EXECUTE with this repository's credentials, rather than
# merely being tested by CI.
#
# Why this is the control and the workflow check is not: for a merge-queue run
# the workflow is read from the queue branch, which carries the pull request's
# own changes — so a fork can edit the step that is supposed to refuse it. The
# CODEOWNERS that applies to a pull request is always the one on the BASE
# branch ("the pull request will use the CODEOWNERS file from that branch in
# the upstream repository"), so a fork cannot supply the rules that judge it.
#
# This file only REQUESTS review on its own. It blocks merging only if the
# ruleset also enables "Require review from Code Owners" — which is the point,
# and has to be turned on separately.
#
# /tests/ and /flow.sh are deliberately not listed. Both execute, but a
# contributor has to be able to add a test and adjust how it runs; that exposure
# is handled by the queue running with persist-credentials off and no registry
# credential, not by review.

/build/          @FalkorDB/falkordb-core
/.github/        @FalkorDB/falkordb-core

# Listed so weakening the rules above needs the same approval they do.
/CODEOWNERS      @FalkorDB/falkordb-core

[![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1146782921294884966?style=flat-square)](https://discord.gg/6M4QwDXn2w)

# falkordb-py

[![Try Free](https://img.shields.io/badge/Try%20Free-FalkorDB%20Cloud-FF8101?labelColor=FDE900&style=for-the-badge&link=https://app.falkordb.cloud)](https://app.falkordb.cloud)

FalkorDB Python client

see [docs](http://falkordb-py.readthedocs.io/)

## Installation
```sh
pip install FalkorDB
```

## Usage

### Run FalkorDB instance
Docker:
```sh
docker run --rm -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb
```
Or use [FalkorDB Cloud](https://app.falkordb.cloud)

### Synchronous Example 

```python
from falkordb import FalkorDB

# Connect to FalkorDB
db = FalkorDB(host="localhost", port=6379)

# Select the social graph
g = db.select_graph("social")

# Create 100 nodes and return a handful
nodes = g.query(
    "UNWIND range(0, 100) AS i CREATE (n {v:1}) RETURN n LIMIT 10"
).result_set
for n in nodes:
    print(n)

# Read-only query the graph for the first 10 nodes
nodes = g.ro_query("MATCH (n) RETURN n LIMIT 10").result_set

# Copy the Graph
copy_graph = g.copy("social_copy")

# Delete the Graph
g.delete()
```

### Asynchronous Example

```python
import asyncio
from falkordb.asyncio import FalkorDB
from redis.asyncio import BlockingConnectionPool


async def main():

    # Connect to FalkorDB
    pool = BlockingConnectionPool(
        max_connections=16, timeout=None, decode_responses=True
    )
    db = FalkorDB(connection_pool=pool)

    # Select the social graph
    g = db.select_graph("social")

    # Execute query asynchronously
    result = await g.query(
        "UNWIND range(0, 100) AS i CREATE (n {v:1}) RETURN n LIMIT 10"
    )

    # Process results
    for n in result.result_set:
        print(n)

    # Run multiple queries concurrently
    tasks = [
        g.query("MATCH (n) WHERE n.v = 1 RETURN count(n) AS count"),
        g.query('CREATE (p:Person {name: "Alice"}) RETURN p'),
        g.query('CREATE (p:Person {name: "Bob"}) RETURN p'),
    ]

    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    # Process concurrent results
    print(f"Node count: {results[0].result_set[0][0]}")
    print(f"Created Alice: {results[1].result_set[0][0]}")
    print(f"Created Bob: {results[2].result_set[0][0]}")

    # Close the connection when done
    await pool.aclose()


# Run the async example
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

nodes.name: fix(asyncio): Is_Cluster gives the sync probe a sync Retry
nodes.content: Fixes #299. `Is_Cluster` builds a synchronous `redis.Redis` probe from the async pool's `connection_kwargs`. When the async client is created with `retry=`, those kwargs hold a `redis.asyncio.retry.Retry`; the synchronous probe called its coroutine `call_with_retry` without awaiting it and crashed with `TypeError: argument of type 'coroutine' is not iterable`. So no `retry` value worked with the async client. The probe now gets a `redis.retry.Retry` with the same backoff, retry count and supported errors, which are the fields redis-py's `AbstractRetry` itself hashes on. This follows the approach of #235 (translate the async pool's kwargs into what the synchronous constructor accepts). `types-redis` predates `AbstractRetry`, hence the narrow `type: ignore[attr-defined]`. ### Tests - `test_is_cluster_does_not_crash_on_an_async_retry_policy`: against an absent server the probe fails with a connection error, never a `TypeError` (fails on `main`). - `test_async_client_accepts_an_async_retry_policy`: `FalkorDB(retry=...)` runs a query end to end (fails on `main`). Full suite: 108 passed, 2 xpassed against `falkordb/falkordb:v4.18.3`; `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy falkordb/` clean. `pyspelling` was not available locally. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #299. `Is_Cluster` builds a synchronous `redis.Redis` probe from the async pool's `connection_kwargs`, and when the async client was created with `retry=`, those kwargs held an async `Retry` whose `call_with_retry` is a coroutine that the sync probe never awaited. The probe now receives a synchronous `redis.retry.Retry` with the same backoff, retry count, and supported errors, so `retry=` works end to end with the async client. Written for commit e48adcb496d78e4f6e65e03e5e202f6111a4a91c. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Fixed an error that could occur when using asynchronous retry policies with cluster detection. * FalkorDB clients configured with asynchronous retry policies can now run queries and close cleanly.

nodes.name: asyncio: Is_Cluster crashes when the client is given a retry policy
nodes.content:
### What happens

Passing the documented `retry=` argument to the async client fails before any query runs:

```python
from falkordb.asyncio import FalkorDB
from redis.asyncio.retry import Retry
from redis.backoff import NoBackoff

FalkorDB(host="localhost", port=6379, retry=Retry(NoBackoff(), 0))
```

```
falkordb/asyncio/cluster.py, in Is_Cluster
    return "redis_mode" in info and info["redis_mode"] == "cluster"
TypeError: argument of type 'coroutine' is not iterable
RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'Retry.call_with_retry' was never awaited
```

### Why

`Is_Cluster` builds a synchronous `redis.Redis` probe from the async pool's `connection_kwargs`. When the caller passed `retry=`, those kwargs hold a `redis.asyncio.retry.Retry`, whose `call_with_retry` is a coroutine. The synchronous probe calls it and never awaits it, so `info()` returns a coroutine.

Passing a synchronous `redis.retry.Retry` instead does not help either: the probe then works, but the async connections get a retry object whose `call_with_retry` is not awaitable. So there is currently no `retry` value that works with the async client, even though the async client is the only way to keep the documented `socket_timeout` plus a bounded retry policy. (redis-py's default retries the connect step 10 times with exponential backoff; against an unreachable server with `socket_timeout=1` we measured 11 attempts over ~15 s.)

### Versions

falkordb 1.7.1 (also current `main`), redis 8.1.0, Python 3.12.

A fix in the same style as #235 (translate the async pool's kwargs into what the synchronous probe accepts) follows in a PR.

Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next Release

Mypy 2.4

We've just uploaded mypy 2.4.0 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features, performance improvements and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

Python 3.15 Support

Mypy 2.4 supports running on Python 3.15 and type checking most Python 3.15 features. This includes the new builtin sentinel type for sentinel values (PEP 661), which mypy now supports (see below for details). Lazy imports (PEP 810) and unpacking in comprehensions (PEP 798) are also supported. Closed TypedDicts (PEP 728) have been supported since mypy 2.2, but the extra_items TypedDict argument, also introduced in PEP 728, is still unsupported. Support for extra_items will be added in a future mypy release.

Native Parser Enabled by Default

Mypy now uses the new native parser by default. It's based on the Ruff parser, and it's significantly faster than the legacy parser, which uses the stdlib ast module. The native parser also has other benefits:

  • You can target newer Python versions and use recent Python syntax even when running mypy on an older Python version. For example, you can use --python-version 3.15 when running mypy on Python 3.14.
  • Stub files can use syntax that is newer than the target Python version. For example, stubs can use the PEP 695 generic class syntax (class Box[T]: ...) when running on or targeting Python 3.10.
  • Parallel type checking requires the native parser.

The legacy parser is still available through --no-native-parser, or native_parser = False in the config file (native_parser = false under [tool.mypy] in pyproject.toml). We are planning to remove the legacy parser in early 2027. If you run into a problem with the native parser, please report it on the issue tracker.

nodes.name: build(deps): update urllib3 requirement from >=2.7.0 to >=2.8.0
nodes.content:
Updates the requirements on [urllib3](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3) to permit the latest version.
Release notes

Sourced from urllib3's releases.

2.8.0

🚀 urllib3 is fundraising for HTTP/2 support

urllib3 is raising ~$40,000 USD to release HTTP/2 support and ensure long-term sustainable maintenance of the project. If your company or organization uses Python and would benefit from HTTP/2 support in Requests, pip, cloud SDKs, and thousands of other projects please consider contributing financially to ensure HTTP/2 support is developed sustainably and maintained for the long-haul.

Thank you for your support.

Security

Fixed the following security issues:

  • The TLS configuration for HTTPS proxies could be ignored or overridden. (High severity, GHSA-8988-9cw3-xx77)
  • HTTPResponse.stream() and read_chunked() could buffer a chunk-size line of unbounded length in memory. (High severity, GHSA-vxq7-64xx-v4gw)
  • Chunked Deflate streaming could enter an infinite loop. (Medium severity, GHSA-gh4c-6fx4-qh6g)

[!IMPORTANT] urllib3 2.8.0 fixes HTTPS proxy TLS configuration being ignored or overridden by destination settings. Configurations relying on that behavior may require changes.

Configure proxy CA certificates and client certificates in proxy_ssl_context, and proxy identity checks with proxy_assert_hostname or proxy_assert_fingerprint. Destination client certificates and identity overrides no longer apply to HTTPS forwarding proxy connections.

[!NOTE] CVE IDs had not yet been assigned to these advisories at the time of release due to a backlog at GitHub's CNA.

Deprecations & Removals

  • Deprecated using an empty collection as the Retry option allowed_methods to retry any verb. (#5044)

Features

  • Added Url.auth_decoded and Url.auth_decoded_joined convenience properties to the result of parse_url(). (#4945)
  • Added basic_auth_encoding and proxy_basic_auth_encoding parameters to urllib3.util.make_headers(). (#5092)

Bugfixes

  • Fixed response header handling to replace obsolete folded header lines (obs-fold) with spaces in accordance with RFC 9112, preventing raw CRLF sequences from appearing in header values such as Set-Cookie. (#1362)

  • Fixed usage of proxy_ssl_context with ProxyManager when use_forwarding_for_https=True. Passing ssl_context instead of proxy_ssl_context for HTTPS proxies in this configuration now emits a FutureWarning and will raise an error in v3.0. (#2577)

  • Changed behavior of the default ConnectionPool.pool initialization. LifoQueue is now resolved from the queue module after the ConnectionPool is instantiated instead of using the default cached QueueCls class property. This is done because sometimes the queue.LifoQueue is monkey-patched late in the program, such as by gevent. (#3289)

  • Raised UnrewindableBodyError instead of ValueError when retrying a request whose body had tell() but not seek(). (#3779)

  • Decoded percent-encoded SOCKS proxy credentials before authenticating with the proxy server. (#3785)

  • Fixed HTTPResponse.drain_conn() to discard unread response data in 64 KiB chunks (same as the default amt when doing HTTPResponse.stream(...)). (#5019)

  • Fixed is_ipaddress() to detect non-standard IPv4 forms accepted by socket.connect, such as hex (0x7f000001), octal (0177.0.0.1), and decimal integers (2130706433), ensuring SSL certificate verification uses the correct mode for these addresses. (#5029)

  • Fixed HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen raising a misleading FullPoolError instead of ValueError when called with an invalid timeout argument on a pool created with block=True. (#5059)

  • Fixed port-zero handling to preserve explicit :0 values instead of substituting the default ports 80 or 443 in URL parsing, pool selection, proxy configuration, connection_from_url(), and HTTP/2 request authority. (#5071, #5101)

  • Fixed a bug where PoolManager passed the assert_hostname and assert_fingerprint parameters to HTTP connection pools. (#5077)

  • Fixed HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen() and HTTP proxy forwarding to strip URL fragments from absolute request targets before sending requests. (#5079)

  • Added safeguards to the proxy tunneling code to prevent potential security issues when handling invalid characters in the proxy host and HTTP headers. This change affects users of Python 3.10, Python 3.11, and Python 3.12 when the standard library does not contain the fix; those on newer Python versions should upgrade to 3.13.14+ or 3.14.5+ to get the same security fixes. (#5091)

  • Fixed HTTPSConnection.connect() overriding ProxyConfig.ssl_context's certificate policy and proxy identity checks with the target connection's TLS settings when forwarding through an HTTPS proxy.

    HTTPSConnection no longer applies target SNI, assertions, or client credentials to forwarding proxy handshakes and continues to use its ssl_context as a fallback when an HTTPS proxy forwards an HTTP target. (#5093)

  • Fixed URL parsing to more strictly enforce RFC 3986 host syntax, rejecting invalid host input such as raw spaces and control characters, malformed percent-encodings, and percent-encoded control characters in HTTP(S) hosts and IPv6 zone identifiers, including proxy CONNECT tunnel targets. Host normalization now also follows RFC 3986 normalization rules for percent-encoded octets by decoding percent-encoded unreserved characters and uppercasing the hexadecimal digits of retained percent-encoded octets. nodes.name: fix(build): restore Maven 3.9.16 so snapshot deploys authenticate
nodes.content: Fixes the failing **Publish Snapshot** run for 0.13.1-SNAPSHOT: https://github.com/FalkorDB/JFalkorDB/actions/runs/37579580314/job/112656056284 ``` Failed to deploy artifacts: Could not transfer artifact com.falkordb:jfalkordb:jar:0.13.1-20261007.060539-1 from/to central (https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/): HTTP Status: 401 ``` ### Cause #455 moved the wrapper to Maven 3.10.0. With `central-publishing-maven-plugin` 0.11.0 (the latest), Maven 3.10.0 deploys snapshots **without credentials**: when Central answers 401, the plugin never retries with the `central` server's username/token. This was the first snapshot deploy since the bump: the 0.13.0 release and the 0.12.1-SNAPSHOT deploy both ran on 3.9.16. PR CI can't catch it because nothing authenticates to Central before the post-merge deploy. ### Reproduction I pointed `-DcentralSnapshotsUrl` at a local server that answers 401 to any request without an `Authorization` header and logs the credentials it receives: | Maven | Result | |---|---| | 3.9.16 | `GET maven-metadata.xml` → 401 → retried with `user:token`; all PUTs authenticated; BUILD SUCCESS | | 3.10.0 | `GET maven-metadata.xml` → 401 → no retry; `HTTP Status: 401`; BUILD FAILURE | This branch: BUILD SUCCESS, 24/24 PUTs authenticated. ### Change - `.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties`: back to Maven 3.9.16 (with its SHA-256). - `.github/dependabot.yml`: ignore `org.apache.maven:apache-maven` `>= 3.10.0`, with a comment explaining how to verify a newer Maven before lifting the hold. After merge, the snapshot workflow should publish 0.13.1-SNAPSHOT. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Restores the Maven wrapper to 3.9.16 so snapshot deploys to Central authenticate again, fixing the 401 failure on the 0.13.1-SNAPSHOT publish. **Changes** - Maven 3.10.0 with `central-publishing-maven-plugin` 0.11.0 sends snapshots without credentials and never retries Central's 401, so the post-merge `Publish Snapshot` job fails. - Dependabot now ignores `apache-maven >= 3.10.0` until a newer release is verified against a 401-answering server, since PR CI never authenticates to Central and cannot catch this. Written for commit 8fe4a3cfd8792c4255cea61d096302aae341964b. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Chores** * The project’s Maven tooling now uses version 3.9.16. * Automated Maven updates to version 3.10.0 and above are on hold pending verification.

nodes.name: Fix audit workflow failure when `NVD_API_KEY` is empty
nodes.content:
The `audit` GitHub Actions job was failing before CVE analysis because OWASP dependency-check treats an empty `NVD_API_KEY` as an invalid key (`length 0`). This change ensures empty values are normalized to “unset” so the audit can proceed without authenticated NVD access when no key is configured.

- **Root cause addressed**
  - `NVD_API_KEY` could be exported as an empty string in CI/manual runs.
  - dependency-check interprets this as a malformed API key and exits fatally.

- **Behavior change (minimal, targeted)**
  - Updated `Justfile` `audit` recipe to unset `NVD_API_KEY` when blank before invoking Maven.
  - No change to behavior when a valid key is present.

- **Implementation**
  ```bash
  if [ -z "${NVD_API_KEY:-}" ]; then unset NVD_API_KEY; fi; \
  ./mvnw -B -Pquality -DskipTests -Dgpg.skip=true org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check
  ```
