nodes.name: SET Clause: Updating Properties and Labels in Cypher
nodes.content:
---
title: "SET Clause: Updating Properties and Labels in Cypher"
sidebarTitle: "SET"
description: "SET is used to create or update properties on nodes and relationships."
---

The `SET` clause is used to create or update properties on nodes and relationships.

## Setting a Single Property

To set a property on a node:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH "MATCH (n { name: 'Jim' }) SET n.name = 'Bob'"
```

## Setting Multiple Properties

You can set multiple properties in a single `SET` clause by separating them with commas:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (n { name: 'Jim', age:32 })
SET n.age = 33, n.name = 'Bob'"
```

## Setting Properties from a Map

You can set properties using a map. There are two operators with different behaviors:

### Replace All Properties (`=`)

Replaces **all** existing properties with the map properties:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (n { name: 'Jim', age:32 })
SET n = {age: 33, name: 'Bob'}"
```

**Result:** The node will have only the properties `age` and `name`. Any other existing properties are removed.

### Merge Properties (`+=`)

Updates only the specified properties while keeping other existing properties:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (n { name: 'Jim', age:32 })
SET n += {age: 33}"
```

**Result:** The node's `age` is updated to 33, but `name` and any other properties remain unchanged.

## Copying Properties Between Entities

You can copy all properties from one entity to another:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (jim {name: 'Jim'}), (pam {name: 'Pam'})
SET jim = pam"
```

After executing this query, the `jim` node will have exactly the same properties as the `pam` node (all of Jim's original properties are replaced).

## Removing Properties

To remove a property, set its value to `NULL`:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH "MATCH (n { name: 'Jim' }) SET n.name = NULL"
```

This removes the `name` property from the node entirely.
## Frequently Asked Questions

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is the difference between SET n = map and SET n += map?">
    The `=` operator **replaces all** existing properties with the map values. The `+=` operator **merges** properties, updating only specified keys while keeping other existing properties intact.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can I remove a property using SET?">
    Yes. Setting a property to NULL removes it: `SET n.name = NULL`. This is equivalent to using the REMOVE clause.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can I copy properties from one node to another?">
    Yes. Use `MATCH (a), (b) SET a = b` to copy all of `b`s properties to `a`, replacing any existing properties on `a`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can I SET multiple properties at once?">
    Yes. Separate property assignments with commas: `SET n.age = 33, n.name = 'Bob'`. All assignments are applied in a single operation.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

nodes.name: CALL Clause: Invoking Procedures and Subqueries in Cypher
nodes.content:
---
title: "CALL Clause: Invoking Procedures and Subqueries in Cypher"
sidebarTitle: "CALL"
description: "The CALL {} (subquery) clause allows local execution of subqueries, which opens the door for many comfortable and efficient actions on a graph."
---

The CALL \{\} (subquery) clause allows local execution of subqueries, which opens the door for many comfortable and efficient actions on a graph.

The subquery is executed once for each record in the input stream.

The subquery may be a returning or non-returning subquery. A returning subquery may change the amount of records, while a non-returning subquery will not.

The variables in the scope before the CALL \{\} clause are available after the clause, together with the variables returned by the subquery (in the case of a returning subquery).

Variables may be imported from the outer scope **only** in an opening `WITH` clause, via simple projections (e.g. `WITH n, m`), or via `WITH *` (which imports all bound variables). The variables returned from a subquery may not override existing variables in the outer scope.

The CALL \{\} clause may be used for numerous purposes, such as: Post-`UNION` processing, local environment for aggregations and actions on every input row, efficient operations using a limited namespace (via imports) and performing side-effects using non-returning subqueries. Let's see some examples.

* Post-`UNION` processing.

We can easily get the cheapest and most expensive items in a store and set their `of_interest` property to `true` (to keep monitoring the 'interesting' items) using post-`UNION` processing:

  ```bash
  GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
  CALL {
    MATCH (s:Store {name: 'Walmart'})-[:SELLS]->(i:Item)
    RETURN i AS item
    ORDER BY price ASC
    LIMIT 1
    UNION
    MATCH (s:Store {name: 'Walmart'})-[:SELLS]->(i:Item)
    RETURN i AS item
    ORDER BY price DESC
    LIMIT 1
  }
  SET item.of_interest = true
  RETURN item.name AS name, item.price AS price
  ```

We can utilize post-`UNION` processing to perform aggregations over differently-matched entities. For example, we can count the number of customers and vendors that a store interacts with:

  ```bash
  GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
  CALL {
    MATCH (s:Store {name: 'Walmart'})-[:SELLS_TO]->(c:Customer)
    RETURN c AS interface
    UNION
    MATCH (s:Store {name: 'Walmart'})-[:BUYS_FROM]->(v:Vendor)
    RETURN v AS interface
  }
  RETURN count(interface) AS interfaces
  ```

* Local environment for aggregations and actions on every input row.

Another key feature of the CALL \{\} clause is the ability to perform isolated aggregations on every input row. For example, let's check if there is any correlation between the amount of sales per-product and the advertisement-intensity implemented for it in a particular month.

  ```bash
  GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
  MATCH (item:Item)
  CALL {
    WITH item
    MATCH (item)-[s:SOLD_TO {advertisement_intensity: 10}]->(c:Customer)
    WHERE s.date > '01-01-2023' AND s.date < '01-02-2023'
    RETURN count(s) AS item_sales_ads_high
  }
  CALL {
    WITH item
    MATCH (item)-[s:SOLD_TO {advertisement_intensity: 5}]->(c:Customer)
    WHERE s.date > '01-01-2023' AND s.date < '01-02-2023'
    RETURN count(s) AS item_sales_ads_low
  }
  RETURN item.name AS name, item_sales_ads_high as high_ads_sales, item_sales_ads_low as low_ads_sales
  ```

* Side-effects.

We can comfortably perform side-effects using non-returning subqueries. For example, we can mark a sub-group of nodes in the graph holding some shared property. Let's mark all the items in a Walmart store that were sold more than 100 times as popular items, and return **all** items in the store:

  ```bash
  GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
  MATCH (item:Item)
  CALL {
    WITH item
    MATCH (item)-[s:SOLD_TO]->(c:Customer)
    WITH item, count(s) AS item_sales
    WHERE item_sales > 100
    SET item.popular = true
  }
  RETURN item
  ```
## Frequently Asked Questions

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is a CALL \{\} subquery?">
    CALL \{\} allows local execution of a subquery for each input row. It enables post-UNION processing, isolated aggregations, and side-effects within a larger query.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="How do I import variables into a CALL \{\} subquery?">
    Variables from the outer scope must be imported via an opening `WITH` clause inside the subquery, e.g. `CALL { WITH n MATCH (n)-[r]->() RETURN count(r) AS rels }`. You can also use `WITH *` to import all bound variables.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can CALL \{\} change the number of result rows?">
    A **returning subquery** (with RETURN) can change the row count. A **non-returning subquery** (without RETURN) preserves the same number of rows, making it ideal for side-effects.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can I use UNION inside CALL \{\}?">
    Yes. CALL \{\} supports post-UNION processing, allowing you to combine results from multiple MATCH patterns and then apply further operations like aggregation or SET on the unified results.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

nodes.name: SKIP Clause: Pagination Offsets in Cypher
nodes.content:
---
title: "SKIP Clause: Pagination Offsets in Cypher"
sidebarTitle: "SKIP"
description: "The optional skip clause allows a specified number of records to be omitted from the result set."
---

The optional skip clause allows a specified number of records to be omitted from the result set.

```cypher
SKIP <number of records to skip>
```

This can be useful when processing results in batches. A query that would examine the second 100-element batch of nodes with the label `Person`, for example, would be:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p ORDER BY p.name SKIP 100 LIMIT 100"
```
## Frequently Asked Questions

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What does SKIP do in a Cypher query?">
    SKIP omits a specified number of records from the beginning of the result set. It is typically used together with LIMIT for pagination.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Should I use ORDER BY with SKIP?">
    Yes. Without ORDER BY, the order of results is non-deterministic, so SKIP may return different records on each execution. Always combine SKIP with ORDER BY for consistent pagination.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="How do I paginate results in FalkorDB?">
    Use `ORDER BY` with `SKIP` and `LIMIT` together. For example, to get page 3 with 100 items per page: `ORDER BY n.name SKIP 200 LIMIT 100`.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

nodes.name: WITH Clause: Query Pipeline Chaining and Aggregations
nodes.content:
---
title: "WITH Clause: Query Pipeline Chaining and Aggregations"
sidebarTitle: "WITH"
description: "The WITH clause allows parts of queries to be independently executed and have their results handled uniquely."
---

The `WITH` clause allows you to chain query parts together, passing results from one part to the next. This enables complex query composition and data manipulations.

## Use Cases

`WITH` is useful for:
- Chaining multiple query parts together
- Performing intermediate aggregations
- Filtering or transforming results before the next query part
- Using query modifiers (`DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, `SKIP`) mid-query

## Example: Filtering by Aggregated Values

Find all children above the average age of all people:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (p:Person) WITH AVG(p.age) AS average_age MATCH (:Person)-[:PARENT_OF]->(child:Person) WHERE child.age > average_age return child"
```

## Example: Using Modifiers Mid-Query

You can use query modifiers with `WITH` to filter or sort before continuing:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (u:User)  WITH u AS nonrecent ORDER BY u.lastVisit LIMIT 3 SET nonrecent.should_contact = true"
```

This query:
1. Matches all users
2. Orders them by last visit (oldest first)
3. Limits to the 3 least recent visitors
4. Sets a flag on those users

## Key Points

- `WITH` acts like a pipeline between query parts
- Variables not included in `WITH` are not available in subsequent parts
- You can rename variables using `AS` in the `WITH` clause
- Aggregations in `WITH` cause implicit grouping (like `RETURN`)
- `WHERE` filters placed after a `WITH` boundary are evaluated **after** any write operations that preceded the `WITH`. This means the filter sees the post-write graph state — for example, it will not see edges that were deleted earlier in the same query.
## Frequently Asked Questions

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What does the WITH clause do?">
    WITH acts as a pipeline between query parts, passing results from one section to the next. It enables intermediate aggregations, filtering, sorting, and variable scoping within a single query.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Do variables carry over after WITH?">
    Only variables explicitly listed in the WITH clause are available in subsequent query parts. Any variable not included is dropped from scope.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can I use ORDER BY and LIMIT with WITH?">
    Yes. WITH supports all query modifiers including DISTINCT, ORDER BY, SKIP, and LIMIT. This lets you filter and sort intermediate results before continuing the query.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="How does aggregation work in WITH?">
    Aggregation functions in WITH cause implicit grouping, just like in RETURN. Non-aggregated expressions become grouping keys automatically.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

nodes.name: LIMIT Clause: Restricting Result Rows in Cypher
nodes.content:
---
title: "LIMIT Clause: Restricting Result Rows in Cypher"
sidebarTitle: "LIMIT"
description: "Can use the limit clause to limit the number of records returned by a query"
---

Although not mandatory, you can use the limit clause
to limit the number of records returned by a query:

```sql
LIMIT <max records to return>
```

If not specified, there's no limit to the number of records returned by a query.
## Frequently Asked Questions

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Is there a default limit on query results?">
    No. If you do not specify a LIMIT clause, FalkorDB returns all matching records with no upper bound.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Does LIMIT improve query performance?">
    LIMIT can reduce the amount of data transferred to the client, but due to a known limitation, it does not currently short-circuit eager operations like CREATE, SET, or DELETE. The full operation executes before LIMIT is applied.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can I use LIMIT without ORDER BY?">
    Yes, but the subset of results returned will be non-deterministic. Combine LIMIT with ORDER BY for predictable, repeatable results.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

nodes.name: MATCH Clause: Querying Graph Patterns in Cypher
nodes.content:
---
title: "MATCH Clause: Querying Graph Patterns in Cypher"
sidebarTitle: "MATCH"
description: "Match describes the relationship between queried entities, using ascii art to represent pattern(s) to match against."
---

The `MATCH` clause describes the relationship between queried entities using ASCII art to represent pattern(s) to match against.

**Syntax Overview:**
- Nodes are represented by parentheses `()`
- Relationships are represented by brackets `[]`
- Each graph entity (node/relationship) can contain an alias, a label/relationship type, and filters, but all are optional

**Entity Structure:** `alias:label {filters}`

Where:
- `alias` - Optional variable name to reference the entity
- `label` - Optional label for nodes or type for relationships  
- `{filters}` - Optional property filters

Example:

```cypher
(a:Actor)-[:ACT]->(m:Movie {title:"straight outta compton"})
```

`a` is an alias for the source node, which we'll be able to refer to at different places within our query.

`Actor` is the label under which this node is marked.

`ACT` is the relationship type.

`m` is an alias for the destination node.

`Movie` destination node is of "type" movie.

`{title:"straight outta compton"}` filters for nodes where the title property equals "straight outta compton".

In this example, we're querying for actor entities that have an "ACT" relationship with the movie entity "straight outta compton".

It is possible to describe broader relationships by composing a multi-hop query such as:

```cypher
(me {name:'swilly'})-[:FRIENDS_WITH]->()-[:FRIENDS_WITH]->(foaf)
```

Here we're interested in finding out who my friends' friends are.

Nodes can have more than one relationship coming in or out of them, for instance:

```cypher
(me {name:'swilly'})-[:VISITED]->(c:Country)<-[:VISITED]-(friend)<-[:FRIENDS_WITH]-(me)
```

Here we're interested in knowing which of my friends have visited at least one country I've been to.

## Variable length relationships

Nodes that are a variable number of relationship→node hops away can be found using the following syntax:

```cypher
-[:TYPE*minHops..maxHops]->
```

`TYPE`, `minHops` and `maxHops` are all optional and default to type agnostic, 1 and infinity, respectively.

When no bounds are given the dots may be omitted. The dots may also be omitted when setting only one bound and this implies a fixed length pattern.

Example:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (charlie:Actor { name: 'Charlie Sheen' })-[:PLAYED_WITH*1..3]->(colleague:Actor)
RETURN colleague"
```

Returns all actors related to 'Charlie Sheen' by 1 to 3 hops.

## Bidirectional path traversal

If a relationship pattern does not specify a direction, it will match regardless of which node is the source and which is the destination:

```cypher
-[:TYPE]-
```

Example:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (person_a:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person_b:Person)
RETURN person_a, person_b"
```

Returns all pairs of people connected by a `KNOWS` relationship. Note that each pair will be returned twice, once with each node in the `person_a` field and once in the `person_b` field.

The syntactic sugar `(person_a)<-[:KNOWS]->(person_b)` will return the same results.

The bracketed edge description can be omitted if all relations should be considered: `(person_a)--(person_b)`.

## Named paths

Named path variables are created by assigning a path in a MATCH clause to a single alias with the syntax:
`MATCH named_path = (path)-[to]->(capture)`

The named path includes all entities in the path, regardless of whether they have been explicitly aliased. Named paths can be accessed using [designated built-in functions](#path-functions) or returned directly if using a language-specific client.

Example:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH p=(charlie:Actor { name: 'Charlie Sheen' })-[:PLAYED_WITH*1..3]->(:Actor)
RETURN nodes(p) as actors"
```

This query will produce all the paths matching the pattern contained in the named path `p`. All of these paths will share the same starting point, the actor node representing Charlie Sheen, but will otherwise vary in length and contents. Though the variable-length traversal and `(:Actor)` endpoint are not explicitly aliased, all nodes and edges traversed along the path will be included in `p`. In this case, we are only interested in the nodes of each path, which we'll collect using the built-in function `nodes()`. The returned value will contain, in order, Charlie Sheen, between 0 and 2 intermediate nodes, and the unaliased endpoint.

## Frequently Asked Questions

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What does the MATCH clause do in FalkorDB?">
    The `MATCH` clause uses ASCII-art pattern syntax to find nodes and relationships in the graph that satisfy the specified pattern. It is the primary read operation in Cypher.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can I traverse variable-length paths with MATCH?">
    Yes. Use the syntax `-[:TYPE*minHops..maxHops]->` to match paths of varying length. Both bounds are optional and default to 1 and infinity respectively.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="What is a bidirectional relationship pattern?">
    A relationship pattern without a direction arrow (e.g. `-[:KNOWS]-`) matches regardless of which node is source or destination. The shorthand `<-[:KNOWS]->` produces the same result.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="How do named paths work?">
    Assign a MATCH pattern to a variable with `p = (a)-[r]->(b)`. The path variable `p` includes all nodes and relationships in the matched pattern and can be used with built-in functions like `nodes(p)` and `relationships(p)`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Do I need to specify labels and aliases in MATCH?">
    No. All parts of the entity structure (`alias:label {filters}`) are optional. However, specifying labels improves query performance by narrowing the search scope, especially when indexes exist on those labels.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

nodes.name: MERGE Clause: Match or Create Graph Patterns in Cypher
nodes.content:
---
title: "MERGE Clause: Match or Create Graph Patterns in Cypher"
sidebarTitle: "MERGE"
description: "The MERGE clause ensures that a path exists in the graph (either the path already exists, or it needs to be created)."
---

The MERGE clause ensures that a path exists in the graph (either the path already exists, or it needs to be created).

MERGE either matches existing nodes and binds them, or it creates new data and binds that.

It’s like a combination of MATCH and CREATE that also allows you to specify what happens if the data was matched or created.

For example, you can specify that the graph must contain a node for a user with a certain name.

If there isn’t a node with the correct name, a new node will be created and its name property set.

Any aliases in the MERGE path that were introduced by earlier clauses can only be matched; MERGE will not create them.

When the MERGE path doesn't rely on earlier clauses, the whole path will always either be matched or created.

If all path elements are introduced by MERGE, a match failure will cause all elements to be created, even if part of the match succeeded.

The MERGE path can be followed by ON MATCH SET and ON CREATE SET directives to conditionally set properties depending on whether or not the match succeeded.

## Merging nodes

To merge a single node with a label:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH "MERGE (robert:Critic)"
```

To merge a single node with properties:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH "MERGE (charlie { name: 'Charlie Sheen', age: 10 })"
```

To merge a single node, specifying both label and property:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH "MERGE (michael:Person { name: 'Michael Douglas' })"
```

## Merging paths

Because MERGE either matches or creates a full path, it is easy to accidentally create duplicate nodes.

For example, if we run the following query on our sample graph:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MERGE (charlie { name: 'Charlie Sheen '})-[r:ACTED_IN]->(wallStreet:Movie { name: 'Wall Street' })"
```

Even though a node with the name 'Charlie Sheen' already exists, the full pattern does not match, so 1 relation and 2 nodes - including a duplicate 'Charlie Sheen' node - will be created.

We should use multiple MERGE clauses to merge a relation and only create non-existent endpoints:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MERGE (charlie { name: 'Charlie Sheen' })
 MERGE (wallStreet:Movie { name: 'Wall Street' })
 MERGE (charlie)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(wallStreet)"
```

If we don't want to create anything if pattern elements don't exist, we can combine MATCH and MERGE clauses. The following query merges a relation only if both of its endpoints already exist:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"MATCH (charlie { name: 'Charlie Sheen' })
 MATCH (wallStreet:Movie { name: 'Wall Street' })
 MERGE (charlie)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(wallStreet)"
```

## On Match and On Create directives

Using ON MATCH and ON CREATE, MERGE can set properties differently depending on whether a pattern is matched or created.

In this query, we'll merge paths based on a list of properties and conditionally set a property when creating new entities:

```bash
GRAPH.QUERY DEMO_GRAPH
"UNWIND ['Charlie Sheen', 'Michael Douglas', 'Tamara Tunie'] AS actor_name
 MATCH (movie:Movie { name: 'Wall Street' })
 MERGE (person {name: actor_name})-[:ACTED_IN]->(movie)
 ON CREATE SET person.first_role = movie.name"
```

## Frequently Asked Questions

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is the difference between CREATE and MERGE?">
    **CREATE** always creates new entities. **MERGE** first checks if a matching pattern already exists; if found it binds to existing entities, otherwise it creates them. MERGE prevents duplicates.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="How do I avoid creating duplicate nodes with MERGE?">
    Use separate MERGE clauses for each entity rather than merging a full path. For example: `MERGE (a {name: 'Alice'}) MERGE (b {name: 'Bob'}) MERGE (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)` ensures no duplicate nodes.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="What are ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET?">
    These directives let you conditionally set properties depending on whether MERGE created a new entity or matched an existing one. For example, `ON CREATE SET n.created = timestamp()` only runs when a new node is created.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Can MERGE create relationships between previously matched nodes?">
    Yes. Use MATCH to bind existing nodes, then MERGE the relationship: `MATCH (a {name: 'Alice'}) MATCH (b {name: 'Bob'}) MERGE (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)`. This creates the relationship only if it does not already exist.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

docs(agentic-memory): add OpenClaw integration page
nodes.content:
## Summary

The docs site had **zero** mentions of OpenClaw, despite two working integration paths that give an [OpenClaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) assistant persistent, graph-structured memory on FalkorDB. This adds a single page documenting both.

Context: [Curing AI Amnesia](https://www.falkordb.com/blog/curing-ai-amnesia/).

### Why `agentic-memory/`

- The value proposition for OpenClaw is long-term agent memory — exactly this section's subject.
- Precedent: `agentic-memory/graphiti-mcp-server.mdx` is already an AI-host integration page (Claude Desktop, Cursor IDE) in this group.
- Both parents already live here: `mem0.mdx` and `cognee.mdx`.
- Rejected `genai-tools/` (LLM frameworks) and `integration/` (data connectors and wire protocols) as wrong categories.

## Changes

- **New** `agentic-memory/openclaw.mdx`, covering both paths at equal depth with a comparison table (memory engine, FalkorDB's role, isolation model, runtime, setup effort, maintainer, when to pick each):
  - **Option A — Mem0 plugin**: `@falkordb/openclaw-mem0`, architecture, install, OSS-mode and FalkorDB Cloud config, platform mode, the five agent memory tools, memory scopes, graph inspection.
  - **Option B — Cognee integration**: why the stock image cannot work via env vars alone, the `sitecustomize.py` / `Dockerfile` / `docker-compose.yaml` recipe, the critical adapter-registration check, `cognee-openclaw` wiring, per-agent graphs, operations and cleanup.
  - Troubleshooting, resources, next steps, and a FAQ accordion, matching sibling-page house style.
- `docs.json` — register the page in the Agentic Memory group, after `agentic-memory/mem0`.
- `agentic-memory/index.mdx`, `mem0.mdx`, `cognee.mdx` — cross-links.
- `.wordlist.txt` — add `OpenClaw`, `openclaw`, `OpenClaw's`, `WhatsApp` for the aspell job.

Accuracy: both npm packages verified live against the registry — `@falkordb/openclaw-mem0@0.4.1` and `@falkordb/mem0@0.2.0`. Cognee version pins are reproduced from the upstream skill along with its "bump deliberately" caveat. Only placeholder credentials appear; the skill's login snippet was not reproduced verbatim.

## Testing

Run locally, all green:

- `node scripts/check_mdx.mjs` — 195 files, 0 syntax errors
- `npx mint@latest broken-links` — no broken links
- `pyspelling -c .spellcheck.yml` — passed
- `python3 -c "import json; json.load(open('docs.json'))"` — valid

Rendered on `mint dev` and verified: 4 tables, 23 code blocks, 3 callouts, 6 accordions with correct anchor IDs, and the sidebar entry resolving from sibling pages. The mermaid block produces output identical to the existing `integration/n8n.mdx` diagram (client-rendered in both cases).

No redirects needed — new path, no legacy `.html` ancestor. Aggregation needs no change; `scripts/aggregate_docs.py` prefixes root-relative links automatically.

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — documentation only.

## Review corrections

Review surfaced several factual errors in the first draft, all verified against primary sources and fixed in `3518ea2`:

- **Node.js prerequisite** — said 22+, but OpenClaw's `engines.node` is `>=24.16.0 <25 || >=26.1.0`. Node 22 cannot run it.
- **Install command** — npm 12 and 11.16+ block lifecycle scripts, so the global install needs `--allow-scripts=openclaw`.
- **Missing plugin install** — Option B configured `cognee-openclaw` without ever installing it. The published package is the scoped `@cognee/cognee-openclaw`; the config key stays short.
- **Hook flags** — both `allowConversationAccess` and `allowPromptInjection` are required; they gate different hook groups, and a missing `allowConversationAccess` fails silently.
- **Intro claim** — originally said `memory-core` re-reads whole files each turn. It is file-backed and searchable; the real gap is the absence of graph edges.
- **Durability** — Option A's default in-process vector store loses embeddings on restart while the graph survives; now warned, with `qdrant`/`chroma` as the fix.
- **Contradictions** — the Compose FalkorDB container clashes with a manually started one, and the "both containers present" check contradicted the Cloud path.

## Related Issues

N/A

  * Added OpenClaw references, recommendations, and links throughout the agentic memory documentation.

nodes.name: Make Cypher cheat sheet examples runnable as shown
nodes.content:
Follow-up to #566. These review fixes were pushed about a minute after that PR was squash-merged, so they never made it into `main`.

All six come from the suppressed findings in [this Copilot review](https://github.com/FalkorDB/docs/pull/566#pullrequestreview-5205300580) and the rounds before it. The common thread is examples that read as runnable but aren't.

| Fix | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Kurt'})` before the `CREATE (a)-[:MEMBER]->(...)` example | `a` was never bound, so the line failed with an unknown-variable error |
| `SET` / `REMOVE` blocks introduced as clause forms, plus one complete worked statement | Every variable in them is unbound; the page's own convention says blank-line-separated statements are independent queries, which implied these were runnable |
| Fuzzy search documented as `%term%distance` with a `%Jangle%1` example | The page said only "`%` for fuzzy matching", so a reader would write `%Jangle` and get nothing. `/cypher/indexing/fulltext-index` specifies `%term%distance`, distance 1–3 |
| Relationship vector example now creates a `REVIEWED` edge before querying | It created the index and queried it but never inserted data, so it always returned zero rows |
| `CALL` added to the vector FAQ snippet | Copying it produced invalid Cypher; every other procedure example on the page includes `CALL` |
| Note that the `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` plan assumes a range index on `:Person(age)` | The sample output shows `Index Scan`, but nothing in the example creates that index — on a fresh graph you get `Node By Label Scan` |

## Validation

Node isn't available in this environment, so the CI checks were approximated with an equivalent Python script: no unescaped `{`, `}`, or `<` outside code; all 42 internal links resolve; 100 fences balanced; `docs.json` still valid and the page still registered. `Jangle` sits inside a fenced block, which pyspelling ignores, so it needs no wordlist entry.

Leaving CI to confirm `validate` and `check-spelling`.

  - Added setup context for vector-search relationship examples.
  - Documented `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` behavior when no range index is available.
  - Corrected vector-search FAQ examples to use `CALL` for procedure invocations.

nodes.name: Add Cypher cheat sheet quick-reference page
nodes.content:
## Why

"Cypher cheat sheet" is one of the highest-volume search queries in the graph database ecosystem, and the docs had no single-page quick reference — the syntax was spread across ~25 separate clause, function, and indexing pages.

## What

Adds `cypher/cheat-sheet.mdx`, a one-page quick reference covering:

- **Patterns** — nodes, relationships, direction, variable-length paths, named paths
- **Reading clauses** — `MATCH`, `OPTIONAL MATCH`, `WHERE`, `RETURN`, `WITH`, `UNWIND`, `UNION`
- **Filtering** — full comparison/string/boolean operator table, pattern predicates, label predicates
- **Writing clauses** — `CREATE`, `MERGE` (with `ON CREATE SET` / `ON MATCH SET`), `SET` (`=` vs `+=`), `REMOVE`, `DELETE` / `DETACH DELETE`, `FOREACH`
- **Subqueries** — `CALL {}` with variable import and side-effect forms
- **Functions** — category table plus aggregation, list/pattern comprehensions, `CASE`, `reduce`
- **Indexing** — range, full-text, and vector index DDL, options table, and drop/list syntax
- **Vector search** — `vecf32()`, `db.idx.vector.queryNodes` / `queryRelationships`, distance functions
- **Constraints, procedures, and graph algorithms**
- **Data types** including temporal, `LOAD CSV`, parameters, and the `GRAPH.*` commands
- **Gotchas** — FalkorDB-specific behaviors (`<>` not indexed, `LIMIT` vs eager operations, relationship uniqueness, no regex operator, no label expressions)

Every example was written against the existing reference pages in this repo rather than generic Cypher, so the syntax matches what FalkorDB actually supports. Each section links out to its full reference page for depth.

### Navigation vs. search intent

Mintlify renders `title` as the sidebar label *and* the H1/SEO title, which forces a tradeoff between a short nav entry and a heading that matches search intent. This page decouples the two:

```yaml
title: "Cypher Cheat Sheet: Query Syntax Quick Reference"
sidebarTitle: "Cheat Sheet"
```

The nav entry stays short next to its `MATCH` / `WHERE` / `MERGE` siblings, while the title carries the terms people actually search for.

### Also

- Registers the page in `docs.json` as the first entry in the Cypher Language group.
- Links it from the Cypher landing page (`cypher/index.mdx`).
- Includes an FAQ accordion group, consistent with the other Cypher pages.

### Review feedback

Every review thread is addressed and resolved:

- **Unbound variables.** The `CASE` and vector-distance examples now include their `MATCH` bindings, and the comprehension / `CASE` / `reduce` block is split so each construct is its own runnable query.
- **Vector dimensions.** The Vector search section is self-contained: it creates a `dimension: 3` index and uses 3-element vectors throughout, instead of querying a 768-dimension index with a 3-element `vecf32()` literal. The index DDL section keeps realistic dimensions on separate labels.
- **Result ordering.** Cosine queries sort `ORDER BY score DESC`; a `<Tip>` explains that euclidean scores are distances and sort ascending.
- **Unique constraint prerequisite.** The supporting multi-property index is created before the `UNIQUE` constraint, and constraints are described as enforced gradually while `UNDER CONSTRUCTION`, ending at `OPERATIONAL` or `FAILED`.
- **Duplicate index creation.** The full-text `OPTIONS` variant is an alternative rather than a second `CREATE` of the same index; the same bug in the range index block is fixed by moving the legacy syntax into prose.
- **Plan operator name.** `Node By Label Scan`, matching the real `GRAPH.PROFILE` output, not `Label Scan`.
- **Multi-query blocks.** PageRank / `SPpaths` and the three `LOAD CSV` variants are now separate fences, and a note up front states that statements separated by a blank line are independent queries.
- **Temporal arithmetic and UDFs.** The FAQ no longer contradicts `/datatypes` or `/udfs`: the `+` / `-` operators work on temporal values, and user-defined functions are available through the Flex UDF library.
- **Shell safety.** The parameter example is single-quoted so `$name` reaches FalkorDB instead of being expanded by the shell.

Shell fences use `bash` rather than `sh`. This is scoped to the new page — the existing `sh` fences elsewhere in the repo are left alone to keep the diff reviewable.

## Validation

Node isn't available in this environment, so the CI checks were approximated locally with an equivalent Python script (valid JSON; no unescaped `{`, `}`, or `<` outside code; all 42 internal links and the `#import_folder` anchor resolve; fences balanced).

CI confirms it on the final commit: `validate` (MDX compile + `mint broken-links`), `check-spelling`, CodeQL, and CodeRabbit all pass.

nodes.name: docs: complete FAQ coverage (193/193) and sharpen question phrasing for AI answer engines
nodes.content:
## Summary

Brings FAQ coverage from **186/193 → 193/193 pages** and fixes question phrasing that breaks when AI answer engines extract an accordion on its own.

## 1. Verified the 7 pages missing FAQs — all of them should have one

I checked each of the 7 pages without an `<AccordionGroup>` rather than assuming. All seven document a distinct product surface with genuine recurring questions (call syntax, install steps, capability limits, troubleshooting), so each got an FAQ grounded strictly in what the page already documents:

| Page | FAQs | Representative questions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `algorithms/harmonic-centrality` | 8 | difference vs. closeness centrality, why a node scores 0, are scores exact |
| `algorithms/maxflow` | 7 | multiple sources/sinks, which edge property is the capacity, performance |
| `browser/canvas` | 8 | React/Vue usage, does Canvas query FalkorDB directly, large-graph tuning |
| `genai-tools/graphify` | 7 | `--falkordb-push` vs `--falkordb`, does re-pushing duplicate nodes |
| `genai-tools/graphrag-sdk` | 9 | SDK vs. GraphRAG Server, incremental updates, why GraphRAG over vanilla RAG |
| `integration/n8n` | 7 | does the node reach FalkorDB directly (no — via GraphRAG-Server), token setup |
| `support` | 5 | how to contact support, what to include in a ticket, where to report a bug |

Notable: several answer a real misconception the page only states implicitly — e.g. the n8n node talks to GraphRAG-Server's REST API, **not** to FalkorDB directly, and Canvas is a rendering component you feed via `setData()`.

## 2. Audited all 742 existing FAQ questions

The existing corpus is in good shape — 741/742 were already well-formed conversational interrogatives. The real gap was a narrow set whose **subject was a pronoun or a bare definite article**. These read fine in page context but become meaningless when Google AI Overviews or Perplexity lift the accordion out of the page, which is exactly the citation path we want to win.

14 rewrites:

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| Does it support transactions? | Does **Spring Data FalkorDB** support transactions? |
| Is the search case-sensitive? | Is **flex.text.indexOf** case-sensitive? |
| Is the comparison case-sensitive? | Is **flex.text.jaroWinkler** case-sensitive? |
| Does it replace all occurrences or just the first? | Does **flex.text.replace** replace all occurrences or just the first? |
| What separators does it recognize? | What separators does **flex.text.upperCamelCase** recognize? |
| Are all characters lowercased? | Does **flex.text.snakeCase** lowercase every character? |
| Can the delimiter be an empty string? | Can the **flex.text.join** delimiter be an empty string? |
| Does the order of elements matter? | Does the order of elements matter in **flex.sim.jaccard**? |
| A property is missing from the list. Why? | **Why is** a property missing from the Schema view? |
| Is Browser access role-based? | Is **FalkorDB Browser** access role-based? |
| Are user-defined functions supported? | Does **FalkorDB** support user-defined functions? |
| What data types are supported? | What data types does **FalkorDB** support? |
| What does maxIterations control? | What does the maxIterations parameter control **in CDLP**? |
| Is weightProp required? | Is weightProp required **for algo.SSpaths**? |

`A property is missing from the list. Why?` was also the only question in the repo that wasn't phrased as a leading interrogative — it now matches how someone would actually type the query.

I deliberately left questions like *"Why is my data lost when I restart the container?"* alone. They lack a product noun but are already strong natural-language queries; adding "FalkorDB" would make them read like keyword stuffing.

## 3. Review feedback — verified against upstream, then fixed

Each point was checked against the actual package metadata and upstream READMEs rather than taken at face value.

**Graphify install commands (`genai-tools/graphify.mdx`)** — the FAQ and the Install section had diverged into two different commands. Both now use `pip install "graphifyy[falkordb]"`. Worth noting the review's premise was partly off: `[falkordb]` is **not** an unsupported extra — PyPI lists it under `provides_extra`, and it pulls in the `falkordb` SDK. The genuine bug was the bare `pip install graphifyy`, which omits that SDK and makes `--falkordb-push` fail with an `ImportError`. The pip form matches the Graphify README (which never mentions FalkorDB at all, so it can't govern the extra).

**GraphRAG-SDK PDF extra (`genai-tools/graphrag-sdk.mdx`)** — correct and worth fixing. `[litellm]` does not include `pypdf`; only the `pdf` extra does. Both the quick start and the FAQ ingest a PDF, so following either as written would fail. Now `[litellm,pdf]`, with a note that the extra is only needed for PDF.

**n8n node categories (`integration/n8n.mdx`)** — correct. The upstream README states that **FalkorDB GraphRAG** appears under the _FalkorDB_ category while the **FalkorDB GraphRAG Tool** variant is listed under _Tools_ for AI Agents. Fixed in both the FAQ and the pre-existing install line, which carried the same error.

**`algo.maxFlow` FAQ title** — rephrased so it reads as a question when extracted standalone.

## Verification

Both of the repo's documented validation commands pass:

```
$ node scripts/check_mdx.mjs
193 files, 0 with syntax errors

$ mint broken-links
success no broken links found
```

Additional checks:

- **193/193** pages contain an FAQ section (was 186/193)
- **793** FAQ questions total; **100%** end in `?` and open with an interrogative
- No remaining pronoun- or article-subject questions
- All CI checks green, including `check-spelling` (needed `HyperLogLog` added to `.wordlist.txt` — the term already existed on `main` inside a blockquote, which the spellcheck config ignores)

Content-only change; no `docs.json` navigation updates needed since all 7 pages were already registered.

- **Documentation**
  - Added FAQ sections to algorithm, Canvas, Graphify, GraphRAG-SDK, n8n, and support documentation.
  - Expanded guidance on setup, usage, compatibility, performance, configuration, and troubleshooting.
  - Clarified FAQ wording across algorithm, browser, Cypher, Spring Data, and text-function documentation.
  - Documented Cypher query parameters, supported data types, and user-defined function support.
- **Chores**
  - Added `HyperLogLog` to the dictionary word list.
